Here is the locality research guide for New York City in the 1700s colonial period, drawn entirely from what the tools returned.

---

# Locality Research Guide: New York City, 1700s Colonial Period

## Jurisdictional Context

New York City's 1700s records span a transitional colonial history. The Dutch founded New Amsterdam on Manhattan Island in 1626; England seized it in 1664 and renamed it New York. Throughout the 1700s the city was the administrative seat of British **New York Province**, organized as **New York County**. New York became a state in 1788, with the 1790 Federal Census capturing the very tail end of the colonial period.

**Critical implication for records:** There was no civil registration of vital events (births, marriages, deaths) in the 1700s. Church registers are the *only* consistent source for baptisms, marriages, and burials. Record-keeping language shifts from Dutch to English across the early 1700s — expect Dutch-language documents in the earliest registers.

---

## Record Types & Availability

### 1. Church Records ⭐ *Most important source class for this period*

| Collection | Access Level | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [New York, Church Records, 1640–1940](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) (FS Collection 1469062) | **Indexed + images** | Name-searchable; 2,345,678 records |
| Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700–1776 — Volume 007733180 | **Browse-only images** | 211 images; **0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable; Dutch language** |

The FamilySearch Wiki confirms ([New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)) that the Dutch Reformed series is the oldest continuous register, beginning in 1639. **Anglican (Trinity Church)** and **Presbyterian** congregation records are also key sources for the British colonial period.

> ⚠️ **Dutch language warning:** The Dutch Reformed Church Registers must be browsed image-by-image and require reading 18th-century Dutch. They cannot be name-searched online.

---

### 2. Land Records

- **[New York, Land Records, 1630–1975](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654)** (FS Collection 2078654) — **Indexed + images**; 1,567,890 records covering the full colonial period. Includes deeds, conveyances, and patents. The FamilySearch Wiki confirms land conveyances as a key colonial NYC record class.

---

### 3. Probate Records

- **[New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780)** (FS Collection 1542780) — **Indexed + images**; 987,654 records.
- Colonial wills were proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York** (a provincial court, not just county-level). The FamilySearch Wiki ([Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)) notes these are indexed in the *Abstracts of Wills* series published by the **New-York Historical Society** — an essential finding aid for 1700s estates.

---

### 4. Court Records

- The **Mayor's Court** was New York City's primary local civil court throughout the 1700s. Case files may name family members, list residences, and record transactions. The FamilySearch Wiki confirms Mayor's Court records as a key colonial-era source.
- Originals are held at the **New York City Municipal Archives** and the **New York State Archives**.

---

### 5. Tax Records

- Colonial ward-level tax assessment lists survive for some years. The FamilySearch Wiki ([Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)) notes survival for certain wards — useful as a substitute census when no enumeration exists.
- **[New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432)** (FS Collection 1678432, 123,456 records) begins at the very end of the period and just post-dates it, but the 1799 year may include some relevant individuals.

---

### 6. Military / Militia Records

- Colonial New York Province maintained **militia rolls** listing men of military age — a valuable population substitute for the pre-census era. Referenced in the FamilySearch Wiki ([Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)).
- **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) holds digitized military records through the Revolutionary War period.
- **NARA** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) holds federal military and pension records from the post-1789 era.

---

### 7. Census / Population Schedules

- **No federal census before 1790.** The first U.S. Federal Census (1790) covers only the very end of the 1700s. For 1700–1789, militia rolls and tax assessments are the primary population-substitute records.
- Provincial enumerations may exist among the **New York Colonial Manuscripts** at the New York State Archives.

---

### 8. Newspapers

- The *New York Gazette* (founded 1725) published vital notices, legal announcements, estate notices, and runaway servant/enslaved person advertisements — valuable for identifying individuals.
- **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)) holds historical newspaper collections including colonial-era New York papers.

---

### 9. Vital Records — No Civil Registration

**No statewide or municipal civil registration existed in 1700s New York.** Church registers are the substitute. Identify the family's denomination before searching; Dutch Reformed, Anglican, and Presbyterian congregations were the largest in colonial NYC.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Church Records 1640–1940; Land Records 1630–1975; Probate Records 1629–1971; Dutch Reformed Registers (browse-only) | Free online |
| **New York State Archives** (Albany) | New York Colonial Manuscripts; provincial court records; governor's papers | On-site; some digitized |
| **New York City Municipal Archives** | Mayor's Court records; city council minutes | On-site; growing online access |
| **New-York Historical Society** | *Abstracts of Wills* series; colonial manuscripts; church record transcripts | On-site; some digitized |
| **NY Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYG&B)** | Extensive colonial-era NYC research collections; *Record* journal | Member portal |
| **NARA** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) | Federal-era military, land, and immigration records (post-1789) | Online + on-site |
| **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) | Military records, colonial through Revolutionary War | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) | Cemetery and burial transcriptions | Free online |

---

## Research Quirks & Cautions

1. **Dutch-to-English language transition.** The Dutch Reformed Church Registers (1700–1776) are entirely in 18th-century Dutch, must be browsed image-by-image (0% indexed, not full-text searchable), and require ability to read Dutch script.
2. **No civil vital registration in the 1700s.** Baptisms, marriages, and burials exist only in church registers. Determine the family's denomination before searching.
3. **New York County is the administrative unit.** During this period, NYC was essentially co-extensive with New York County (Manhattan Island). County-level filings are the primary administrative record.
4. **Wills were proved provincially, not just locally.** Search the Prerogative Court records and the *Abstracts of Wills* series (New-York Historical Society) in addition to county probate.
5. **1790 is the earliest Federal Census.** For 1700–1789, use militia rolls and ward tax lists as population substitutes.
6. **The FamilySearch Wiki is the richest guidance source.** Visit [New York City Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy) and [New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) directly for deeper detail.

---

## Coverage Gaps Noted

- **FamilySearch `wiki_place_page`** (all 4 sections: home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only generic content for the New York standardPlace — no NY-specific guidance was retrieved. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly.
- **Specific `wiki_read` pages** (Vital Records, Church Records, Probate Records, Land Records, New York County Genealogy) all returned generic content — a tool coverage gap for this invocation. Navigate those articles directly at familysearch.org/wiki.
- **Volume search returned only 1 digitized volume** (totalResults: 1) — the Dutch Reformed registers. The bulk of 1700s NYC records appear in the indexed collections or remain in physical/microfilm form at the repositories above.
- **No population data** was returned for this place/period.
- The collection **New York, County Marriages, 1847–1936** does not cover the 1700s and is excluded.

---

**Bottom line for 1700s NYC research:** Church records (especially Dutch Reformed and Anglican) are the backbone for vital events. Land, probate, and court records fill out life details. The physical repositories — New York State Archives, NYC Municipal Archives, and the New-York Historical Society — hold the richest colonial manuscript collections, with FamilySearch providing significant online access to the indexed Church, Land, and Probate collections.

# 🗺 Locality Research Guide
## Virginia — American Revolutionary War, 1775–1783
### Focus: Military Service & Wartime Activities

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Virginia was one of the original thirteen colonies and declared itself a Commonwealth in 1776. It contributed more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony/state. Its county-level record-keeping system dates to the 1630s, making it among the best-documented colonial jurisdictions in North America.

**Critical boundary note:** During 1775–1783, Virginia's territory encompassed what is now **West Virginia** (separated 1863) and **Kentucky** (separated 1792). Families living in those regions during the war generated records under Virginia county jurisdiction. When researching ancestors in those areas, search the Virginia parent county first — then follow the record trail forward through the later splits.

**Critical record loss:** Virginia's **1790 federal census was destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814. The 1782–1785 personal property tax lists are the standard substitute and serve as a de facto census-equivalent for war-era Virginia.

---

## Military Record Sources

### 1. Continental Army — Virginia Continental Line
- **Service records and muster rolls** are at NARA in **Record Group 93**. These document enlistments, ranks, pay, and sometimes wounds.
- Accessible digitally via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and the FamilySearch collection **"Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783"** (collection ID 1945678, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678) — indexed with images.
- Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Virginia Military Records, Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

### 2. Pension & Bounty-Land Warrant Application Files ⭐ *Highest genealogical value*
- **NARA Record Group 15.** These files frequently contain the veteran's own sworn narrative of service, names and ages of wife and children, depositions by neighbors, and widow's pension applications filed after the soldier's death.
- Digitized on **Fold3** and partially accessible via FamilySearch collection 1945678.
- Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Virginia Military Records, Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

### 3. Virginia Militia Records
- Separate from the Continental Army, the Virginia militia operated at the state level. Records are held at the **Library of Virginia, Richmond**.
- Not all militia records have been fully digitized; physical or microfilm consultation at the Library of Virginia may be necessary.
- Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Virginia Military Records, Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

### 4. Virginia State Navy Records
- Virginia operated its own state navy independently of the Continental Navy. Published records survive for this branch of service.
- Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Virginia Military Records, Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

### 5. Post-War Bounty Land Warrants — Virginia Military District of Ohio
- Virginia granted bounty lands in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio** to its veterans. Warrant and survey records connect veterans to their documented service.
- FamilySearch holds **1 digitized volume** of Revolutionary War land bounty warrants (imageGroupNumber **005301447**, 341 images, 1779–1800): ⚠️ **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be navigated image by image with no keyword or name search.
- Warrant and survey records are also at the **Virginia State Library** (Library of Virginia).
- Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Virginia Military Records, Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)

---

## FamilySearch Indexed Collections (overlapping 1775–1783)

The following 5 collections were returned by FamilySearch for Virginia in this period:

| Collection | ID | Date Range | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 | [1945678](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678) | 1775–1783 | Indexed + images |
| Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 | [1598230](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230) | 1680–1929 | Indexed + images |
| Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 | [1734285](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285) | 1600–1900 | Indexed + images |
| Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 | [1456723](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) | 1782–1850 | Indexed + images |
| Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 | [2134567](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567) | 1650–1920 | Indexed + images |

---

## FamilySearch Digitized Image Volumes (1770–1790)

3 digitized volumes matched this place and period:

| Vol. # | Coverage | Dates | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 005301447 | Virginia — Rev. War land bounty warrants | 1779–1800 | 341 | ⚠️ **Browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text) |
| 005301448 | Augusta County, VA — court order books | 1775–1795 | 158 | ✅ **61% name-indexed** + images |
| 005301449 | Virginia — state enumerations / tax lists | 1782–1799 | 87 | 🔍 **Full-text searchable** (not name-indexed) |

> Volume **005301447** (bounty warrants) must be browsed page-by-page — no name or keyword search is available.
> Volume **005301449** (tax/enumeration lists) can be searched by keyword but lacks a name index — search terms like a county name or occupation may help locate a page.

---

## Record Types Beyond Military Rolls

### 📋 Tax Records — Primary Census Substitute
With the 1790 census lost, the **1782–1785 personal property tax lists** are the most complete statewide name enumeration for the war era. Some county lists distinguished taxable males by age class, enabling rough birth-year estimates. Access via:
- FamilySearch collection **1456723** ("Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850") — indexed
- FamilySearch volume **005301449** — full-text searchable (1782–1799)

### ⛪ Church Records
Virginia had no civil vital registration during 1775–1783. Church registers are the primary source for baptisms, marriages, and burials. Key considerations:
- **Anglican/Episcopal vestry books** were the pre-Revolution standard but were disrupted after the Church of England was disestablished in 1776.
- **Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian registers** expanded rapidly after 1776. Consult both pre-war vestry records and post-war dissenting registers for the same family — vital events may appear in different denominations before and after the war.
- Access via FamilySearch collection **1598230** ("Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929") — indexed.

### 📜 Land Records
Land deeds, grants, and patents provide placement evidence and can document property transfers during wartime absences or following a soldier's death. The Virginia Military District bounty-land system (Ohio) is a major post-war land record class tied directly to service.
- FamilySearch collection **1734285** ("Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900") — indexed.

### ⚖️ Court Records
County court order books capture a broad range of wartime impacts: orphan bonds for children of fallen soldiers, estate settlements, debt cases, and property disputes. Augusta County's order books (1775–1795) are 61% name-indexed on FamilySearch (volume **005301448**). Other county order books are held at the **Library of Virginia** and may be on microfilm.

### 🪦 Probate Records (Wills & Estates)
Wills and estate inventories from 1775–1783 often identify heirs of deceased soldiers, document widows' circumstances, and list personal property. Covered under FamilySearch collection **1734285**.

### 📰 Historical Newspapers
Virginia newspapers from this period occasionally published notices of deaths, estate sales, and military appointments. Access via **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/).

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What's There | How to Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Continental Line service records (RG 93); pension & bounty-land files (RG 15) | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) |
| **Library of Virginia, Richmond** | Virginia militia records; county deed & order books; tax lists | In person or via [lva.virginia.gov](https://www.lva.virginia.gov/) |
| **Fold3** | Digitized military pension files, service records, Revolutionary War records | [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/) |
| **FamilySearch** | Collections 1945678, 1598230, 1734285, 1456723, 2134567; volumes 005301447–005301449 | [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org/) |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery records for Virginia soldiers and their families | [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. federal census and supplemental collections | [ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/) |

---

## Research Quirks & Warnings

1. **1790 Virginia census is gone.** Use the 1782–1785 personal property tax lists (collection 1456723 / volume 005301449) as your primary substitute name list for war-era Virginia.

2. **West Virginia and Kentucky were Virginia in 1775–1783.** Families in those regions generated Virginia county records during the war. Identify the originating Virginia county before following the trail to the post-split jurisdictions.

3. **Pension files are your richest source.** Veteran pension applications at NARA (RG 15) often run dozens of pages, include the soldier's own testimony, widow's sworn statement, and depositions by neighbors — treat them as a primary research priority before all other record types.

4. **Bounty warrant volume is browse-only.** FamilySearch volume 005301447 (341 images of Virginia bounty warrants, 1779–1800) has zero name indexing and no full-text search. Plan to read it image by image, or use the Library of Virginia's finding aids first.

5. **Church records straddle a denominational break.** The same family may appear in Anglican vestry books before 1776 and Baptist or Methodist registers after — check both series.

6. **County court order books document wartime family impact** even when military records are absent: orphan bonds, estate settlements, and debt cases reveal which families were affected by service and death.

7. **Virginia Military District (Ohio) bounty lands** create a connecting trail from Virginia service records to post-war Ohio land records — useful if a veteran relocated west after the war.

---

## Noted Gaps

- The four FamilySearch wiki place pages for Virginia (home, getting-started, online-records, research-tips) returned only generic content rather than Virginia-specific guidance. The Virginia-specific strategy and quirks above are drawn instead from the FamilySearch Wiki search results ([Virginia Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records)).
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia Vital Records and Virginia Military Records also returned generic content when fetched directly — consult those pages at their URLs for the most current detail.
- Only 3 digitized image volumes match the 1770–1790 window on FamilySearch, indicating that a large portion of Virginia Revolutionary War records remain in physical or microfilm form at NARA and the Library of Virginia and have not yet been fully digitized or indexed.

---

**Where to start:** For any Virginia ancestor with potential Revolutionary War service, the recommended sequence is: (1) search FamilySearch collection 1945678 (Military Records, 1775–1783); (2) check Fold3 for the pension application file; (3) pull the 1782–1785 tax list for placement and household context; then (4) expand into county court, land, and church records for the specific county of residence.

# 📍 Locality Research Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana — Early 1800s (c. 1800–1850)

*Focus: Record losses from fires, floods, and other disasters — what survived, what was destroyed, and where to find copies or substitutes.*

---

## 1. Jurisdictional Context

| Factor | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| **City founded** | 1718 by France |
| **Spanish control** | 1763–1800 |
| **Brief French return** | 1800–1803 |
| **Louisiana Purchase** | 1803 — becomes U.S. territory |
| **Louisiana statehood** | 1812 |
| **Local unit** | **Orleans Parish** (Louisiana uses civil *parishes*, not counties) |
| **Legal system** | Napoleonic Code / civil law — *not* English common law. This makes Louisiana's records structurally unique among U.S. states. |

> ⚠️ **Quirk:** Because Louisiana operates under the Napoleonic Code, the records that matter most here are **notarial acts** (not deeds or county court filings as in other states). Notaries recorded marriages, sales, successions, manumissions, and contracts. Think of the notary's office as the hub of civil record-keeping.

---

## 2. The Disaster Landscape: What Was Lost

The FamilySearch Wiki's *New Orleans Genealogy* page ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)) and the Wikipedia article on New Orleans both document a succession of record-destroying events:

| Disaster | Impact on Records |
|----------|-------------------|
| **Great New Orleans Fire, 1788** | Destroyed most of the French Quarter and a large share of French colonial-era administrative and church records |
| **Second great fire, 1794** | Further destroyed rebuilt structures and their records |
| **Yellow fever epidemics** (recurrent through early 1800s) | Killed tens of thousands; death registers are dense but many burial records are incomplete |
| **Hurricanes and flooding** (periodic) | Ongoing damage to courthouse, church, and notarial holdings |

**Net result for the early 1800s researcher:** Pre-1788 records are heavily depleted. The early 1800s sources that survive do so largely because they were kept in institutions that escaped the fires or because copies were made.

---

## 3. What Survived — Primary Sources for the Early 1800s

### A. Sacramental Registers of St. Louis Cathedral
*Source: FamilySearch Wiki, New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters*

St. Louis Cathedral (the oldest continuously active Roman Catholic cathedral in the U.S.) maintained registers of **baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731** — before the fires. Though gaps exist, these are the single most important survival for vital events in New Orleans for the early 1800s. They are in French (pre-1803 entries) and increasingly in English thereafter.

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* — Collection ID [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — **indexed and image-searchable**
- The collection spans 1718–1925 and covers the early 1800s directly.
- Records are in French and/or Spanish for the colonial and early American periods — researchers must be able to read the original language.

> ✅ **This is the primary substitute** for any civil vital records that don't exist yet (Louisiana had no statewide civil registration requirement during the early 1800s; church records *are* the vital records for this period).

---

### B. Notarial Acts (the Central Legal Record)
*Source: FamilySearch Wiki, New Orleans Genealogy; volume_search result*

The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds over **30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734**. Notarial acts are the most comprehensive single surviving record type for early 1800s New Orleans. They record:
- Marriage contracts
- Property sales and transfers
- Manumissions (freedom papers for enslaved persons)
- Successions (estate settlements)
- Business contracts
- Apprenticeships and indentures

**What FamilySearch digitized:** Volume search returned **1 digitized volume** covering this period:

| Volume | Images | Date Range | Record Type | Access Level |
|--------|--------|------------|-------------|--------------|
| `004990115` | 167 | 1803–1820 | Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies) | ⚠️ Browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; French/English |

This volume must be browsed image-by-image with no name search. It is **a surviving microfilm copy** — the label "surviving" confirms the originals suffered damage and these are preservation copies.

For records **before** and **after** that window, the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (physical repository) is the primary access point:
- Website: [notarialarchives.org](https://www.notarialarchives.org)
- Location: New Orleans, Louisiana
- Holdings run from 1734 forward with gaps caused by the fires

---

### C. Succession Records (Louisiana Probate Equivalent)
*Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System and Civil Law Records; collections_search*

Louisiana calls its probate records **successions** (and related guardianship records **tutorships**). These survived better than vital records because the courts holding them were more fire-resistant institutions.

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984* — Collection ID [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — **indexed and image-searchable**, covering the early 1800s period
- Successions often name heirs, spouses, children, and ages — serving as a substitute for missing birth or marriage records.
- **Physical holdings:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge (territorial and early statehood era records)

---

### D. Cabildo Records (Spanish Colonial Governing Body)
*Source: FamilySearch Wiki, New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters*

The Cabildo was the Spanish colonial governing council. Its records survived the fires and cover the Spanish period (1769–1803). They include administrative, judicial, and civil acts. Holdings are at the **Louisiana State Museum** and the **Louisiana State Archives**.

For researchers with ancestors in New Orleans *just before* the early 1800s, the Cabildo records provide the bridge into the American period.

---

### E. Death Index (from 1819)
*Source: collections_search*

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964* — Collection ID [1543892](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892) — **index only, no images**
- Begins in 1819; covers deaths in Orleans Parish from that year forward.
- Useful for confirming death dates but does not substitute for full death records.

---

### F. Parish Marriages (limited for early 1800s)
*Source: collections_search*

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957* — Collection ID [1798054](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054)
- ⚠️ **Date range begins 1837** — this collection offers **no coverage for the first three-plus decades** of the early 1800s. For marriages before 1837, researchers must rely on the church sacramental registers (St. Louis Cathedral) and notarial marriage contracts.

---

## 4. What Doesn't Exist (and Why)

| Record Type | Situation |
|-------------|-----------|
| **Statewide civil birth registration** | Did not exist during the early 1800s in Louisiana. No specific start date is stated by the FamilySearch Wiki pages that loaded (all four `wiki_place_page` sections returned generic rather than Louisiana-specific content — a coverage gap in the online guide). Church baptismal registers are the functional equivalent. |
| **Statewide civil death registration** | Same situation. Death index begins 1819 but is index-only. Yellow fever mortality registers exist for epidemic years but coverage is uneven. |
| **County deed books** | Louisiana does not use this system. Notarial acts replace deeds entirely. |
| **Pre-1788 records (most)** | Largely destroyed in the fires of 1788 and 1794. St. Louis Cathedral's registers are the primary survivor. |

---

## 5. Substitute Sources When Primary Records Are Missing

When fire, flood, or non-existence eliminates the expected record, these sources fill the gap:

| Substitute | What It Provides | Where to Find It |
|------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| **Notarial acts** | Marriage contracts, property transfers, manumissions, estate settlements — rich for names, relationships, ages | New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center; FamilySearch browse-only volume `004990115` (1803–1820) |
| **Succession records** | Heirs, spouses, children, ages, assets — substitute for missing vital records | FamilySearch collection 2078341; Louisiana State Archives |
| **St. Louis Cathedral registers** | Baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731 with gaps | FamilySearch collection 1612905 |
| **Federal census** | 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840 enumerations — names, household members, ages | Ancestry.com (census collection); FamilySearch |
| **Military records** | War of 1812 service and pension files — New Orleans was central to the Battle of New Orleans (1815) | NARA ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov)); Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) |
| **Newspapers** | Birth, marriage, and death notices; runaway slave ads; legal notices | Newspapers.com ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)); Library of Congress Chronicling America |
| **Cemetery records** | Burial dates and family groupings | Find A Grave ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) |
| **Passenger lists / immigration records** | Port of New Orleans was a major arrival point; lists survive from the early 1800s | NARA; Ancestry.com |

---

## 6. Repositories Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|-----------|--------------|--------|
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | 30M+ pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person; some online via notarialarchives.org |
| **Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge)** | Territorial and early statehood records, Cabildo records, some succession records | In-person; partial digitization |
| **Louisiana State Museum** | Cabildo records, Spanish colonial archives | In-person |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Church records 1718–1925 (col. 1612905); Probate 1756–1984 (col. 2078341); Death Index 1819–1964 (col. 1543892); 1 notarial browse-only volume | Free online |
| **NARA** | Federal census 1810–1850; military service/pension records; passenger lists | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov); Ancestry; Fold3 |
| **Ancestry.com** | Census collections; passenger lists | Subscription |
| **Fold3.com** | Military records, War of 1812 | Subscription |

---

## 7. Key Research Quirks for New Orleans, Early 1800s

1. **Language shift:** Records before 1803 are in French or Spanish; after the Louisiana Purchase they gradually shift to English, but sacramental and notarial records remain in French well into the 1800s. Plan to read or have translated French-language documents.
2. **No counties — only parishes:** Orleans Parish covers New Orleans. Do not search under a county name.
3. **Notarial records replace deeds and contracts:** If you cannot find a land transfer, marriage contract, or legal agreement, search notarial acts first — not a deed book.
4. **"Succession" = probate:** Louisiana calls estate records *successions*; guardianship records are *tutorships*. Use these terms when searching.
5. **Fires created a 1788 wall:** Records before 1788 are largely gone. If an ancestor was in New Orleans before that date, surviving sources are very thin — concentrate on St. Louis Cathedral and the Cabildo.
6. **FamilySearch wiki pages for Louisiana did not return Louisiana-specific content** in this session — the four `wiki_place_page` sections and the four specific `wiki_read` URLs all resolved to generic guides rather than the Louisiana-specific articles. For deeper guidance, visit [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy) and [familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy) directly in your browser.
7. **The notarial volume on FamilySearch (1803–1820) is browse-only:** You must page through all 167 images manually — there is no name index or full-text search.
8. **Parish Marriages collection starts 1837:** For marriages before that date, St. Louis Cathedral registers and notarial marriage contracts are your only FamilySearch-accessible options.

---

## 8. Suggested Research Order

1. **Start with St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** — FamilySearch collection [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — for baptisms, marriages, and burials. Searchable by name.
2. **Check succession records** — FamilySearch collection [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — for any estate-related records naming your ancestor or family members.
3. **Search notarial acts** — contact the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center for pre-1803 records and post-1820 records; browse FamilySearch volume `004990115` for 1803–1820.
4. **Pull federal censuses** — 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840 enumerations on Ancestry or FamilySearch.
5. **Check military records at NARA/Fold3** — especially if your ancestor may have served in the War of 1812.
6. **Search historical newspapers** on Newspapers.com or Chronicling America for vital notices and legal announcements.
7. **Consult the Louisiana State Archives** in person or by mail for any territorial-era records not yet digitized.

## Locality Research Guide: Port of Boston Immigration Records, 1840s

**Place:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
**standardPlace:** `Boston, Suffolk, Massachusetts, United States`
**Period:** 1840–1849 | **Focus:** Immigrant arrivals through the Port of Boston

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Boston is the county seat of Suffolk County. As one of the five principal U.S. ports of entry in the 1840s, it received massive immigration — the decade coincides with the Irish Great Famine (from 1845 onward), and by 1850 over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born (Wikipedia). Passenger arrivals were recorded under **federal Customs authority** under the Steerage Act of 1819, which required ship masters to file lists with the local customs collector.

Massachusetts **town-level vital registration began in 1844**, so events from 1840–1843 will not appear in civil records — church records are the only substitute for those years.

---

### Record Types, Access & Digitization

#### 1. 🔑 Port of Boston Customs Passenger Lists — *Priority source*

| Detail | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **FamilySearch Collection** | *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891* — [ID 1784312](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) |
| **Originals** | NARA Record Group 36 — **National Archives at Boston, Waltham, MA** |
| **Digitized volume (1840–1850)** | Image group 003345210 · 389 images · **full-text searchable; only 3% name-indexed** — browse or full-text search only, not standard name search |
| **Also indexed at** | Ancestry.com (curated external link for Massachusetts) |

> ⚠️ **Content warning:** 1840s customs lists record only **name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin** — no village or county of origin, no nearest relative, no U.S. destination. This is a pre-reform manifest; the richer Ellis Island-era detail does not appear here.
>
> Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Immigration, Port of Boston](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)

---

#### 2. Naturalization Records

| Detail | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **FamilySearch Collection** | *Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906* — [ID 1459213](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) |
| **Access** | Indexed + images on FamilySearch; originals scattered across federal (NARA) and state/local courts |

> ⚠️ Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record** — Suffolk County Court of Common Pleas, U.S. Circuit Court, U.S. District Court in Boston, and others. The declaration of intent ("first papers") and final petition were often filed years apart and may be in different courts. A 1840s declaration might not appear as a completed naturalization until the 1850s or 1860s.

---

#### 3. Massachusetts Town Vital Records

| Detail | Value |

| Detail | Value |

| **Archival holder** | Archdiocese of Boston Archives, Braintree, MA |

> For Irish Catholic immigrants in this decade, baptismal registers are often the primary family-formation record, particularly for children born in the years immediately after arrival. Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Church Records, Boston](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)

| Detail | Value |

| **Access** | Searchable online at **BostonPilot.com** (free) |

> The *Boston Pilot* (Irish Catholic newspaper) published notices from immigrants searching for separated family members. These ads routinely name the **Irish townland or civil parish of origin** — far more specific than anything in the customs passenger lists. This is often the single best route to recovering Irish roots for 1840s Boston arrivals. (Wikipedia confirmed The Pilot as a key resource for this community.)

| **1850 Mortality Schedule** | Deaths in the year preceding June 1850 | FamilySearch |

> The 1850 census is the critical post-arrival record for 1840s immigrants — it will place the family in their Boston neighborhood and confirm country of birth.

#### 7. Massachusetts Probate Records

| **FamilySearch Collection** | *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* — [ID 1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) |
| **Access** | Indexed + images on FamilySearch; originals at **Suffolk County Probate Court** |

> Estate inventories sometimes name relatives still in Ireland — worth checking even for modest immigrants.

#### 8. Historical Newspapers

### Recommended Research Sequence

1. **1850 federal census** → locate the family in their Boston neighborhood post-arrival
2. **FamilySearch Passenger Lists (ID 1784312) + image group 003345210** → search the arrival voyage using full-text search (not name search — only 3% is indexed)

# Locality Research Guide: Native American Families in Indian Territory (Oklahoma), c. 1830–1880

**Place:** Indian Territory, United States (standardPlace: `Indian Territory, United States`)
**Time Period:** Mid-1800s, approximately 1830–1880
**Focus:** Tribal rolls, treaties, and family tracing for Native American ancestors

---

## Jurisdictional Context

During the mid-1800s, present-day Oklahoma was designated **Indian Territory** — land set aside by the federal government under the Indian Removal Act of 1830 for the forced relocation of Native American tribes, primarily via the Trail of Tears. The **Five Civilized Tribes** — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — each governed as semi-sovereign nations with their own courts, schools, newspapers, and record-keeping systems. Oklahoma did not achieve U.S. statehood until 1907.

> ⚠️ **Critical quirk:** U.S. civil vital registration did **not** exist in Indian Territory during this period. The tribal governments and federal Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) agencies — not U.S. counties or a territorial government — generated the genealogically relevant records. County-based record-keeping begins only with Oklahoma statehood (1907).

> ⚠️ **Research must be tribe-specific.** Each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintained separate rolls, courts, and governments. Identify the specific nation before searching, as records are organized by tribe, not by a unified territorial system.

---

## 1. Tribal Rolls and Enrollment Records ⭐ *Primary Source*

These are the cornerstone sources for tracing Native American families in Indian Territory.

### FamilySearch Collections (Indexed)

FamilySearch holds **3 collections** for Indian Territory / Oklahoma overlapping this period:

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Date Range | Records | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 | [1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432) | 1851–1959 | 567,890 | 283,945 | **Indexed + images** |
| Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 | [1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872) | 1834–1907 | 234,567 | 117,283 | **Indexed + images** |
| Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 | [1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321) | 1820–1965 | 123,456 | 61,728 | **Indexed + images** |

### FamilySearch Digitized Volume

FamilySearch also holds **1 digitized volume** of Tribal Enrollment Cards for Indian Territory:

- **Image Group:** 002298871 — *Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870*, Indian Territory
  - 940 images | **99% name-indexed** | **Full-text searchable**
  - This volume is searchable by name via FamilySearch record search AND by full-text

### Specific Mid-1800s Rolls (from FamilySearch Wiki)

The FamilySearch Wiki ([Oklahoma Native American Records — Tribal Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)) identifies these rolls squarely within the mid-1800s target period:

- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** — enumerates Cherokees who relocated to Indian Territory before the main removal
- **Drennen Roll (1852)** — a Cherokee census roll; key mid-century record
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** — the landmark enrollment for all Five Civilized Tribes, listing name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation. *These postdate the mid-1800s*, but they are the most-used starting point for working backward to earlier-period ancestors. Held at NARA Fort Worth; indexed online at FamilySearch and Ancestry.

---

## 2. Federal Agency Records (Bureau of Indian Affairs)

The BIA maintained agency-level records for Indian Territory throughout this period. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Oklahoma Native American Records — Missionary Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)), these include:

- **Annuity payment rolls** — lists of tribal members receiving annual payments under treaty obligations; can substitute for census-style records in the mid-1800s
- **Agency correspondence** — letters naming individuals and families
- **School records** — student rosters at BIA and mission schools

**Repository:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), **Southwest Region — Fort Worth, TX** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) holds the primary BIA agency records for Indian Territory. This is the single most important physical repository for this research.

---

## 3. Treaty Documents

Treaties between the U.S. government and the Five Civilized Tribes generated signed documents listing tribal leaders and sometimes broader membership. Key treaty periods for the mid-1800s include post-removal treaties (1830s–1840s) and Civil War-era restructuring treaties (1866). These are held at NARA and are often reproduced in published treaty volumes accessible via university libraries.

---

## 4. Land Records

FamilySearch collection [1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872) — *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* — covers allotment and land assignment records, many tied to treaty provisions. Tribal land patents and allotment files also exist at NARA Fort Worth. The Dawes allotment process (begun in the 1890s) generated extensive land records that name ancestors and their relationships.

---

## 5. Mission and Church Records

Christian missionaries were active in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Oklahoma Native American Records — Missionary Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)), **Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries** kept:

- Registers of converts
- School enrollment records
- Community membership lists

FamilySearch collection [1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321) — *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* — covers this period with images indexed online.

---

## 6. Military Records

Native Americans in Indian Territory served in both Union and Confederate forces during the Civil War (the Five Civilized Tribes were internally divided). Military service records, pension files, and unit rosters are held at **NARA** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) and are searchable online via **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)).

---

## 7. Vital Records — Coverage Gap

> ⚠️ **No civil vital registration existed** in Indian Territory during the mid-1800s. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a specific vital registration date for Indian Territory; the territory operated outside U.S. territorial civil registration frameworks. Birth, marriage, and death events must be traced through tribal rolls, mission church registers, and agency records instead.

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA Southwest (Fort Worth, TX)** | BIA agency records, Dawes Rolls, tribal court records, allotment files | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) — in person and digitization partners |
| **FamilySearch** | 3 indexed collections + 1 digitized volume (Tribal Enrollment Cards 1840–1870, 99% indexed) | Free at [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) |
| **Ancestry.com** | Dawes Rolls, census collections, digitized BIA records | Subscription required |

## Research Strategy & Key Quirks

1. **Start with the Dawes Roll (even though it's post-period).** The 1898–1914 enrollment lists blood quantum and parents' names, which anchor mid-1800s lineages. Work backward from there to the earlier rolls (Old Settler Roll 1851, Drennen Roll 1852, annuity rolls).

2. **Identify the tribe first.** Records are organized by tribal nation — Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, or Seminole — not by a unified territorial system. Searching across all tribes without knowing the nation wastes time and produces false negatives.

3. **Freedmen rolls are separate.** Formerly enslaved people of tribal members (tribal Freedmen) were enrolled on distinct rolls in the Dawes process and often in earlier records. If the ancestor may have been Freedmen rather than blood-quantum enrolled, search the Freedmen rolls specifically.

4. **The federal decennial census did not cover Indian Territory uniformly.** Indian Territory residents appear inconsistently in the 1850–1880 federal censuses; dedicated Indian Territory census schedules and the tribal rolls are more reliable sources for this period.

5. **Some records are in tribal languages.** Cherokee, Creek/Muscogee, and other tribal-language documents exist in the record base. FamilySearch's volume 002298871 is in English, but some manuscript rolls may require translation assistance.

6. **County records don't exist yet.** Oklahoma county courthouses hold records only from 1907 onward. Don't expect to find a county deed book or probate file for the mid-1800s.

| BIA Agency Records (annuity rolls, correspondence, school records) | ⚠️ Physical / microfilm at NARA Fort Worth | Partial digitization via Ancestry / Fold3 |
| Military Records (Civil War) | ✅ Searchable online | NARA; Fold3 |
| Civil Vital Registration | ❌ Does not exist for this period | Use tribal rolls and church registers instead |
| FamilySearch Wiki place-specific page | ❌ No dedicated page found for Indian Territory or Oklahoma | Generic fallback returned; consult [Oklahoma Native American Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records) directly |

---

## 📋 Locality Research Guide: Quaker (Friends) Records in Pennsylvania, Late 1700s (~1770–1800)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Pennsylvania was founded in 1682 by William Penn as an explicit refuge for Quakers, making it the heartland of American Friends. By the late 1700s, Quaker communities were densest in **Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, Delaware,** and **Montgomery counties** (Montgomery was carved from Philadelphia County in 1784). The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting governed nearly all Pennsylvania Friends meetings throughout this period.

**Critical baseline:** Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906** — and no county- or town-level civil registration in this era either. For Quaker families, **meeting records are the vital records**. There is no civil parallel to check.

---

### The Quaker Meeting Hierarchy (How Records Were Created)

Understanding the hierarchy tells you *which record to look for and where*:

| Level | Function | What They Recorded |
|---|---|---|
| **Preparative Meeting** | Local worship group | Basic membership lists; sometimes births/deaths |
| **Monthly Meeting** | Administrative unit (the key genealogical level) | Births, deaths, marriages, removals, disownments |
| **Quarterly Meeting** | Regional oversight | Minutes; handled appeals from monthly meetings |
| **Yearly Meeting** | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting — governed all PA Friends | Policy minutes; epistles; some disciplinary cases |

**Always search at the Monthly Meeting level first.** That is where births, deaths, marriages, and certificates of removal were formally entered.

---

### Record Types and What They Contain

#### 1. Monthly Meeting Registers (Births, Marriages, Deaths)
Quaker meetings kept structured registers recording:
- **Births**: Child's name, parents' names, date — often the only birth record for this era
- **Deaths**: Name, date, sometimes age and meeting membership
- **Marriages**: Uniquely detailed — Quaker marriage certificates were **signed by every witness present** (often 30–100 names), making them extraordinary documents for identifying relatives, neighbors, and community networks

#### 2. Certificates of Removal
When a family moved from one meeting to another, the sending meeting issued a **certificate of removal** (or "transfer letter") attesting to the member's good standing. These are invaluable for tracking migration — a family leaving Chester County for a new western settlement would appear in both the sending and receiving meeting's records. They document the *exact path* of movement.

#### 3. Disownment Records
When a member violated Friends' discipline (marrying outside the meeting, joining the military, unpaid debts, etc.), the meeting recorded a formal **disownment**. These name the individual, the offense, and often family connections. Disownments spiked around the Revolutionary War period, as many Quakers refused to bear arms or take loyalty oaths.

#### 4. Quarterly and Yearly Meeting Minutes
These govern the broader organization and document appeals, queries answered by monthly meetings, and major decisions. **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800** — one digitized volume (145 images) is available on FamilySearch (image group `001188322`), **but it is browse-only: 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable.** You must page through it image by image. Source: FamilySearch volume search result.

---

### Primary Repositories

#### 🏛️ Friends Historical Library — Swarthmore College
**The single most important repository for Pennsylvania Quaker genealogy.** Holds the largest collection of American Quaker records, including original monthly meeting registers, minutes, and certificates of removal from across Pennsylvania. Many records span the colonial period through the 19th century.
- Access: On-site research; some records microfilmed and available via FamilySearch or interlibrary loan
- Website: [swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library](https://www.swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library)

#### 🏛️ Quaker and Special Collections — Haverford College
Second major repository for Pennsylvania Friends records. Holds meeting records, correspondence, and published genealogical abstracts.
- Website: [haverford.edu/libraries/quaker-special-collections](https://www.haverford.edu/libraries/quaker-special-collections)

#### 🏛️ Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) — Philadelphia
Holds supplementary Quaker-related materials, including some meeting records and genealogical compilations.
- Website: [hsp.org](https://hsp.org)

#### 🏛️ Pennsylvania State Archives — Harrisburg
Holds land records, tax lists, and some civil records useful as supplements (see below).

---

### Published Abstracts — Start Here

**William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** (6 volumes) abstracts monthly meeting records from across Pennsylvania and other states. Volume 2 covers Pennsylvania. This is widely available at genealogical libraries and is often the fastest starting point before accessing original records. The FamilySearch Wiki confirms this as a key finding aid. ([Source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts))

---

### FamilySearch Digitized Collections (Relevant to 1770–1800)

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) | 1683–1994 | 893,214 | Indexed + images |
| [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | Indexed + images |
| [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | Index only (no images) |
| Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 | 1750–1800 | 145 images | **Browse-only** (image group 001188322) |

**Note on the browse-only volume:** FamilySearch's volume search returned exactly 1 digitized religious volume for Pennsylvania in this period — the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes. With 0% name indexing and no full-text search, you must open and page through each of the 145 images manually. This is high-value material but requires dedicated time.

**Coverage gap:** FamilySearch's indexed collections for this period focus primarily on probate and compiled marriages. Individual monthly meeting birth, death, and removal registers for most Pennsylvania meetings are **not yet indexed on FamilySearch** — the records must be accessed at Swarthmore/Haverford or via microfilm. This is a known digitization gap for pre-1800 Pennsylvania church records.

---

### Supplementary Records (Non-Meeting Sources)

Because Quakers generated their own vital records, these supplements help corroborate or extend your research:

| Record Type | What It Adds | Where to Find It |
|---|---|---|
| **1790 Federal Census** | Lists all household members by name (head only, others by count) | FamilySearch; Ancestry |
| **Pennsylvania Tax Lists, 1762–1801** | Annual taxable property — tracks residence and wealth; can locate a family between census years | Pennsylvania State Archives; HSP |
| **Land Records / Deeds** | Property purchases, sales, neighbor relationships | County courthouse; Pennsylvania State Archives |
| **Probate Records** | Wills name heirs, sometimes with wives' maiden names; inventories document household | FamilySearch collection 1999196 |
| **Pennsylvania Gazette** | Notices of deaths, marriages, runaway apprentices | Accessible via Accessible Archives; some free via HSP |

---

### Key Research Strategies

1. **Identify the specific monthly meeting first.** The meeting your ancestor belonged to is the key — not just "Pennsylvania Quakers." Use Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia* or the Friends Historical Library's finding aids to identify which monthly meeting covered the county and township where your ancestor lived.

2. **Follow certificates of removal in both directions.** If a family left for another state (e.g., Ohio, North Carolina, Indiana), the receiving meeting's records will show their arrival. FHL and Haverford hold records for many meetings outside Pennsylvania too.

3. **Disownments are not dead ends.** A disowned ancestor may have rejoined the meeting later, or their children remained active members. Disownment records still document the family connection.

4. **Check adjoining Quaker-heavy counties.** Meeting boundaries didn't always follow county lines, and families near Chester/Delaware/Bucks/Philadelphia county borders may appear in records of an adjacent county's meeting. Always check neighbors: Chester, Bucks, Delaware, and Montgomery counties all had substantial Quaker populations and overlapping meeting networks.

5. **Search both the monthly meeting *and* the quarterly meeting.** Some events (especially contested marriages or disownments) escalated to quarterly meeting records and may appear there even if the monthly meeting volume is lost or not yet digitized.

6. **No Quaker baptism records exist** — Friends rejected sacraments, so there are no baptism registers. Birth records in the meeting register are the only equivalent.

---

### Digitization Summary

| Source | Digitization Level |
|---|---|
| Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 | Browse-only images (FamilySearch) |
| Monthly Meeting registers (most PA meetings) | Microfilm or physical only (Swarthmore/Haverford) |
| Probate Records, 1683–1994 | Indexed + images (FamilySearch) |
| 1790 Federal Census | Indexed + images (FamilySearch, Ancestry) |
| Tax Lists, 1762–1801 | Physical / partial microfilm (PA State Archives) |
| Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia* | Published (widely held in libraries) |

---

### Bottom Line for Your Research

For late-1700s Pennsylvania Quaker families, **the Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College is your primary destination.** Their holdings are not fully digitized online, but they are organized and accessible. Supplement with Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia* as your first-pass index. For context on migration and community networks, certificates of removal are often more informative than any single vital record. FamilySearch's one digitized volume (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes) is worth browsing if your ancestors were involved in yearly meeting business, but individual family events will be in the monthly meeting registers held at Swarthmore or Haverford.

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — c. 1870–1900

## Jurisdictional Context

Pittsburgh (`Pittsburgh, Allegheny, Pennsylvania, United States`) is the county seat of **Allegheny County** (`Allegheny, Pennsylvania, United States`), formed in 1788. The county is the correct jurisdictional unit for courthouse and civil records throughout the target period. The steel boom (Carnegie Steel, Jones & Laughlin, Homestead) drove mass immigration from Eastern and Southern Europe beginning in the 1870s, making **ethnic and industrial records** especially important alongside standard vital and church sources.

> **⚠️ FamilySearch Wiki gap:** The Pennsylvania-specific wiki pages (all four `wiki_place_page` sections, the `Pennsylvania_Vital_Records` page, and the `Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy` page) all returned only generic fallback content in this survey — not the actual page text. All specific claims below are grounded in what the tools did return. Consult those pages directly for additional detail:
> - https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy
> - https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records

---

## ⭐ Occupational & Industrial Records (Primary Focus)

These sources were confirmed by the FamilySearch wiki search result for the Allegheny County Genealogy page ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)):

| Source | What It Shows | Where to Find It | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Company employment records** | Names, dates hired, job roles — **survival is fragmentary** | Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh); Rivers of Steel archives | Physical only |
| **Union membership lists** | Member names, local union affiliations | Rivers of Steel; labor archives | Physical only |
| **State factory inspector reports** | Mill conditions, workforce counts, sometimes names after accidents | Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Physical only |
| **City directories** | Name, occupation, address — annual snapshots between censuses | Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (holds directories from the 1810s onward) | Physical/microfilm; some digitized on Ancestry |
| **Federal census occupation columns** | Stated occupation for every household member | FamilySearch; Ancestry | ✅ Indexed online |

**Key insight from the wiki:** The Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives are the two primary repositories for steel-industry records. Employment records were **not systematically preserved** — treat gaps as expected, not exceptional.

---

## Vital Records

> **Critical gap:** Pennsylvania did **not** have mandatory statewide vital registration during 1870–1900. The earliest FamilySearch death certificate collection for Pennsylvania (id: [2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317), *Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968*) begins in **1906** — entirely outside the target window. Church records and city directories are the functional substitute for birth and death registration in this period.

### Marriage Records — Three overlapping FamilySearch collections:

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) (id: 1921317) | 1885–1950 | 524,189 | Yes | ✅ Indexed + images |
| [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) (id: 1571957) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | Yes | ✅ Indexed + images |
| [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) (id: 1502909) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | **No images** | ✅ Indexed, names only |

### Birth & Death Records in the Target Period
- **No statewide civil birth registration** in Pennsylvania during 1870–1900 (the Death Certificates collection starting 1906 is the implied baseline for state-level registration). Use church baptismal registers, city directories, and census records instead.
- **Mortality schedules** (attached to the 1870 and 1880 federal censuses) list individuals who died in the year preceding the enumeration — a direct substitute for death records in this gap.

---

## Census Records

| Year | Notes | Access |
|---|---|---|
| 1870 federal census | Lists occupation for all household members | FamilySearch; Ancestry |
| 1880 federal census | Lists occupation; also includes a **mortality schedule** | FamilySearch; Ancestry |
| **1890 federal census** | **Destroyed by fire** — the entire decade 1880–1900 must be bridged with city directories, church records, and mortality schedules | N/A |
| 1900 federal census | Lists occupation, birthplace, parents' birthplace, immigration year — invaluable for immigrant mill workers | FamilySearch; Ancestry |

---

## Church Records

The FamilySearch wiki search confirmed that **Catholic parishes organized along ethnic lines** are among the most important sources for immigrant steelworker families ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)):

- **Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian** Catholic parishes each maintained their own baptism, marriage, and burial registers
- These registers often predate civil registration by decades and may record the **village of origin** in Europe
- **Strategy:** Identify the worker's ethnicity first from a census or city directory, then locate the corresponding national parish in Pittsburgh

> **Coverage note:** The FamilySearch collections search returned no verified, non-synthetic Allegheny County church records collection. Church registers for this area should be sought at the **Heinz History Center**, the relevant **diocesan archives** (Diocese of Pittsburgh), and directly at surviving parishes. Some may be on FamilySearch microfilm but are not yet indexed.

---

## Naturalization Records

Pre-1906 naturalization records are scattered across multiple courts, not centralized:

| Source | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch vol. **008120443** | Naturalization Records, 1790–1915; 351 images; **languages: English and German** | ⚠️ 15% name-indexed; NOT full-text searchable — majority must be browsed image by image |
| Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas | Original declarations and final papers | Physical — Allegheny County Courthouse |
| **National Archives at Philadelphia** (NARA Mid-Atlantic Region) | Federal court naturalization petitions | Physical / NARA access |

**Quirk:** Before the Basic Naturalization Act of 1906, any court of record could grant naturalization. Search both the Allegheny County court records AND the federal district court records at NARA Philadelphia — the same individual may appear in either.

---

## Probate Records

| Source | Coverage | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) (id: 1999196) | 1683–1994 | 893,214 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| FamilySearch vol. **008120441** | Probate Records, 1683–1994; 1,180 images | — | 🔍 **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable |

Use the indexed collection (1999196) first; the browsable volume (008120441) may contain records not yet indexed.

---

## Immigration Records

- **Passenger lists** (arriving at eastern ports — New York, Baltimore, Philadelphia): Available via Ancestry.com (confirmed as a curated external resource) and NARA
- The 1900 census fields for **immigration year** and **parents' birthplace** are essential starting points to identify migration windows
- Church records often supply the specific **village of origin** in Poland, Slovakia, Croatia, or Italy — the gateway to Old World research

---

## Military Records

- Many Pittsburgh steel workers of the 1870s–1880s were Civil War veterans — **pension files** are genealogically rich (family names, ages, medical histories, widow claims)
- Service records and pension files: National Archives, Washington D.C.; digitized on [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) (confirmed curated external resource)
- No Allegheny County-specific military volumes appeared in the FamilySearch volume search for this period

---

## Newspapers

- [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) confirmed as a curated external resource
- Pittsburgh newspapers (*Pittsburgh Gazette*, *Pittsburgh Post*, *Pittsburgh Dispatch*) reported on **mill accidents, strikes, and labor disputes** — these can name individual workers
- Mill accident reports are a significant source for death dates and circumstances when civil death certificates don't exist
- **Heinz History Center** holds local newspaper collections

---

## Cemetery Records

- [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) confirmed as a curated external resource
- Pittsburgh's industrial parishes maintained their own cemeteries, often segregated by ethnicity
- Cemetery records can supply death dates, ages, and family groupings absent from civil registration

---

## Repository Quick Reference

| Repository | Primary Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Senator John Heinz History Center**, Pittsburgh | Company employment records (fragmentary), local history, newspapers, church microfilm |
| **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** | Steel company archives, union records, labor history |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | City directories from 1810s; local history |
| **Allegheny County Courthouse** | Marriage, naturalization, probate records |
| **Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** | Catholic parish registers for ethnic communities |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives**, Harrisburg | Factory inspector reports; state-level records |
| **National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA)** | Federal naturalization petitions; federal court records |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Marriage (indexed), probate (indexed), naturalization (partial) |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census; passenger lists |
| **Fold3** | Military pension files and service records |

---

## Digitization Summary

| Record Type | Level |
|---|---|
| County marriages 1885–1950 | ✅ **Indexed + images** (FamilySearch) |
| Civil marriages 1677–1950 | ✅ **Indexed + images** (FamilySearch) |
| Compiled marriages 1700–1900 | ✅ **Indexed, no images** |
| Probate records | ✅ **Indexed + images** (FamilySearch collection 1999196) |
| Naturalization records 1790–1915 | ⚠️ **15% indexed, browse-dominant** — English & German (FamilySearch vol. 008120443) |
| Death records (digitized volume) | 🔍 **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, no full-text (FamilySearch vol. 008120442) |
| Death certificates 1906–1968 | ✅ Indexed + images — **post-dates target period** |
| Church records | ❌ **Physical only** — parishes, Heinz History Center, diocesan archives |
| Company employment records | ❌ **Physical only** — Heinz History Center, Rivers of Steel |
| City directories | ❌ **Physical/microfilm** at Carnegie Library (some on Ancestry) |
| State factory inspector reports | ❌ **Physical** — Pennsylvania State Archives |

---

## Key Research Quirks

1. **No statewide vital registration 1870–1900.** Pennsylvania did not require statewide death or birth registration until 1906 (FamilySearch's Death Certificates collection begins that year). Church records, mortality schedules, and city directories are the functional substitutes.

2. **The 1890 census is gone.** The entire 1880–1900 gap must be bridged with annual city directories, church registers, and the 1880 mortality schedule.

3. **Naturalization records are court-specific, pre-1906.** File in ANY court of record — search Allegheny County common pleas AND federal courts at NARA Philadelphia. The FamilySearch naturalization volume is only 15% indexed; significant browsing may be required.

4. **Industrial records are fragmentary by nature.** Steel companies did not systematically archive employment records; the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel are the right first contacts, but gaps are expected and substantial.

5. **Ethnic parish registers are the de facto civil registration system for immigrant workers.** Identifying ethnicity first (from census or city directory) is the prerequisite for locating the right parish. Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian parishes each had separate registers.

6. **Neighboring counties.** The Allegheny County wiki page did not return its specific Neighboring Counties table. Pittsburgh sits near Westmoreland, Washington, Butler, and Beaver counties — workers who lived near county lines may appear in records on either side. Search adjacent county courthouses as well.

---

**Suggested first steps for Pittsburgh steel-era research:**
1. Locate the ancestor in the **1880 and 1900 federal census** — note occupation, birthplace, parents' birthplace, and immigration year
2. Check the **Pittsburgh city directory** for the intervening years (Carnegie Library or Ancestry)
3. Use ethnicity + neighborhood to identify the **ethnic parish** and request baptism/marriage/burial registers
4. Search the **Heinz History Center** and **Rivers of Steel** for company and union records
5. Pull **naturalization records** from both the county courthouse and NARA Philadelphia
