The wiki place pages returned generic fallbacks rather than Pennsylvania-specific content — I'll read the specific Philadelphia page from the URL the wiki_search returned, and do a targeted volume search for burial/church/death records.

I now have enough to compile the guide. Here are the findings:

---

## Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — Locality Research Guide
### Families Affected by the 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic
**Period of interest:** 1793 and immediate aftermath (c. 1788–1805 for surrounding records)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Philadelphia was established in 1682 as both a city and a county. In 1793, it was the capital of the United States with a population of approximately 50,000. The city and Philadelphia County were coterminous for most practical purposes at the time. Pennsylvania did **not** have statewide civil registration of births or deaths until **1906**, meaning there are no government-issued death certificates for the epidemic era — church registers and civic committee records are the primary documentary substitutes.

From the Wikipedia article on the epidemic: the outbreak lasted **August–November 1793** and killed approximately **5,000 people**, roughly one-tenth of the population. Thousands more fled the city into surrounding counties and across the Delaware River into New Jersey.

---

### The Epidemic as a Records Event

The 1793 outbreak is unusually well-documented for its era because of the civic crisis it created. According to the FamilySearch Wiki's Philadelphia Genealogy page ([Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)), the key genealogical sources are:

| Source | Type | Access |
|--------|------|--------|
| **Mathew Carey's published account** | Lists names of the dead; printed 1793, widely reprinted | Published/digitized; held at HSP, NARA, and many libraries |
| **Minutes & reports of the Committee appointed by the citizens** | Civic crisis-management body; named individuals aided and deceased | Manuscript; Philadelphia City Archives and HSP |
| **Bush Hill hospital records** | Hospital set up for epidemic victims | Manuscript; Philadelphia City Archives |
| **Church burial registers** | Baptism, marriage, and burial registers by denomination | Scattered — see church records section below |

---

### Record Types and Access

#### 1. Church Records — ⚠️ PRIMARY SOURCE for 1793 Deaths and Burials
With no civil death registration, **church burial registers are the only systematic record of epidemic deaths**. The FamilySearch Wiki's Philadelphia church records section ([Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)) notes that Philadelphia's diverse religious communities each maintained registers; many colonial and early national registers have been **transcribed and published**. The **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)** has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church registers.

Named churches documented in the wiki_search results as holding key burial records from the epidemic era:
- **Christ Church** (Anglican/Episcopal) — one of the most complete pre-1800 burial registers in the city
- **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church)** — one of the oldest churches in the US; holds Lutheran/Swedish burial registers

**FamilySearch digitized volumes:** The volume search found **1 digitized volume** covering Philadelphia in this period:
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800** — Image group `001188322`, 145 images
- Coverage: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
- **Access level: Browse-only images** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be paged through image by image)
- Language: English
- Quaker Meeting records include births, deaths, and disownments

> **Gap to note:** FamilySearch's digitized holdings for Philadelphia church records in this exact era are sparse — only this single Quaker volume appeared in the volume search. Church records from other denominations (Episcopal, Lutheran, Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist, Baptist) are largely held by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania, the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP), and individual churches or their archives.

**Where to look for church records physically or on microfilm:**
- **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)**, Philadelphia — compiled indexes and transcriptions of many Philadelphia church registers; now housed at the HSP
- **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**, 1300 Locust St, Philadelphia — holds original and microfilmed church registers for many Philadelphia congregations
- **Individual denomination archives** — Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia), Catholic Historical Research Center (Philadelphia), etc.

---

#### 2. Probate Records — HIGH VALUE for Epidemic Deaths
A spike in wills and estate administrations in late 1793 directly tracks epidemic mortality. Heads of household who died intestate or left wills created records naming surviving family members, orphaned children, and heirs.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
- **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** — Collection ID `1999196`
  - 893,214 records / 446,607 images
  - Covers the 1793 target period
  - [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)

Philadelphia County's original probate files are also held at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and at the **Register of Wills** office.

---

#### 3. Civil/Government Vital Records — ABSENT for 1793
Pennsylvania's statewide death registration did not begin until **1906** (per the FamilySearch Wiki's Philadelphia Genealogy page). The two statewide death collections found in the collection search — *Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968* (collection `2255317`) — are **outside the target period** and are not useful for 1793 research.

---

#### 4. Marriage Records
Two collections cover the target period and may document family reconstitution after the epidemic (remarriages of widows/widowers, or delayed marriages):

- **Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** — Collection `1571957`, 312,045 records [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957)
- **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** — Collection `1502909`, 198,765 records [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909)

---

#### 5. Census Records
- **1790 Federal Census** — taken 3 years *before* the epidemic; establishes household composition pre-outbreak. Available on Ancestry.com, FamilySearch, and Fold3.
- **1800 Federal Census** — taken 7 years *after* the epidemic; compare with 1790 to identify households that shrank (deaths), disappeared (fled permanently), or relocated within Philadelphia.
- There is no census taken in 1793 itself.

---

#### 6. Newspapers — HIGH VALUE for Named Victims and Refugees
Philadelphia newspapers published death notices and epidemic-related announcements throughout the outbreak. Names of the dead, notices of property sales, and announcements about families who had fled appear extensively.

- **Newspapers.com** — [https://www.newspapers.com/](https://www.newspapers.com/) — holds historical Philadelphia newspapers
- **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, free) — [https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) — may cover some Philadelphia papers

---

#### 7. Land and Property Records
Families fleeing the epidemic often sold or abandoned property. A sudden sale or transfer of Philadelphia real estate in late 1793 can document flight. Conversely, estate sales of property belonging to the deceased document deaths.

- Philadelphia County deed books are held at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and the **Register of Deeds**
- FamilySearch has microfilmed some Pennsylvania land records (check the FamilySearch catalog)

---

#### 8. Military / Federal Records
- **NARA** — [https://www.archives.gov/](https://www.archives.gov/) — holds federal pension files and service records; veterans who died in the epidemic may have widows' pension applications naming family members
- **Fold3** — [https://www.fold3.com/](https://www.fold3.com/) — digitized military records including pension files

---

#### 9. Cemetery Records
- **Find A Grave** — [https://www.findagrave.com/](https://www.findagrave.com/) — searchable cemetery memorial database; covers many Philadelphia historic burying grounds
- Physical burial grounds: Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei churchyard, St. Peter's, and numerous other historic Philadelphia churchyards

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**, 1300 Locust St, Philadelphia | Church registers (originals and microfilm), Mathew Carey's papers, Committee minutes, newspapers | In-person research room; some digitized through HSP |
| **Philadelphia City Archives**, 3101 Market St, Philadelphia | City government records, Bush Hill hospital records, deed books, probate originals | In-person; finding aids online |
| **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)** (collections now at HSP) | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records | HSP reading room |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Quaker Yearly Meeting Minutes (browse-only, group 001188322); Probate 1683–1994; Marriage compilations | Free online; some browse-only |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1790, 1800); additional Pennsylvania collections | Subscription |
| **NARA** | Federal pension files, passenger lists, military records | In-person in Philadelphia region; some digitized on Fold3 |

---

### Neighboring Jurisdictions — Important for Flight Records

Thousands of Philadelphians fled the city during August–November 1793. If your ancestor disappeared from Philadelphia records around that time, search the adjacent counties for burial and church records:

- **Montgomery County, PA** (north) — Germantown was a common refuge destination
- **Delaware County, PA** (southwest)
- **Chester County, PA** (west)
- **Bucks County, PA** (northeast)
- **Burlington County and Gloucester County, NJ** (across the Delaware River)

> **Quirk:** The neighboring counties page for Philadelphia County did not load from the FamilySearch Wiki — the adjoining jurisdictions listed above come from geographic context, not a tool-returned table. Confirm neighbors via the [Philadelphia County Genealogy Wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy) when that page becomes accessible.

---

### Research Quirks and Gotchas

1. **No civil death registration in 1793.** Pennsylvania did not require statewide death registration until 1906. Church burial registers and the Mathew Carey list are the primary documentation of epidemic deaths.
2. **The 1793 "list of the dead" is published.** Mathew Carey's *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever* (1793) includes lists of named dead — check a library holding or a digitized copy before assuming an ancestor is undocumented.
3. **FamilySearch's digitized Philadelphia holdings for this era are sparse.** Only one volume appeared in the volume search: the Quaker Yearly Meeting Minutes (browse-only). Church records from other denominations require visiting HSP, GSP, or the denomination's own archive.
4. **Compare the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses head-to-head.** A household present in 1790 but absent or smaller in 1800 in Philadelphia may reflect epidemic mortality or permanent relocation; check the surrounding county census pages for the same surname.
5. **Probate is a high-yield substitute.** With no death certificates, a Philadelphia County will or administration file from late 1793–1794 is often the most specific documentation of an epidemic death, naming heirs and family members. Use FamilySearch collection `1999196`.
6. **The city and county of Philadelphia were legally distinct.** For 1793, most records were generated at the county level; do not limit searches to "city" only when the tools allow a county choice.

---

### Digitization Level Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Digitization | Physical Location |
|---|---|---|
| Quaker Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 | ✅ Browse-only images (group 001188322) | HSP |
| Probate Records 1683–1994 | ✅ Indexed + images (collection 1999196) | Philadelphia City Archives |
| Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 | ✅ Indexed (collection 1502909) | Scattered |
| Civil Marriages 1677–1950 | ✅ Indexed + images (collection 1571957) | Scattered |
| Church burial registers (non-Quaker) | ⚠️ Sparse — largely physical/microfilm only | HSP, GSP, denomination archives |
| Mathew Carey's published list | ✅ Published — check library digitization | HSP, Ancestry, HathiTrust |
| Committee/Bush Hill records | ❌ Not digitized on FamilySearch | Philadelphia City Archives, HSP |
| Death certificates | ❌ Not available until 1906 | — |
| Federal census 1790/1800 | ✅ Indexed on Ancestry, FamilySearch | NARA |
| Newspapers (1793) | ✅ Newspapers.com; Chronicling America | HSP, Free Library of Philadelphia |

---

**Bottom line:** The 1793 epidemic is unusual in that it generated its own dedicated documentary record — the Mathew Carey list, the Committee minutes, and the Bush Hill hospital files — which exist alongside the normal church burial register series. Start with the Carey publication and HSP's Committee papers, then work through whichever church denomination your ancestor belonged to. FamilySearch's own digitized holdings for this exact time and place are limited to one browse-only Quaker volume, so in-person or mail research at HSP and the Philadelphia City Archives will likely be necessary.

# Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Locality Research Guide
### Focus: Families Affected by the Great Chicago Fire (October 8–10, 1871)
**Time period surveyed:** c. 1840–1900 | **Jurisdiction:** Cook County, Illinois, United States

---

## ⚠️ The Core Problem: The Record Destruction of 1871

The Great Chicago Fire burned October 8–10, 1871, killing approximately 300 people and leaving more than 100,000 residents homeless across roughly 3.3 square miles. The **Cook County Courthouse** — which housed the city's deeds, birth and death registers, court records, probate files, and tax rolls — was completely destroyed. This is the defining fact for Chicago genealogy: **virtually all official pre-1871 records held locally were lost.** Research for fire-era families requires a substitution strategy built around records created or held outside Chicago.

The Illinois legislature responded with the **Burnt Record Act of 1872**, which required property owners to re-register their deeds, creating a new (reconstructed) property record series. Every other record class discussed below must similarly be approached with the pre/post-1871 divide in mind.

---

## Jurisdictional Context

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Jurisdiction | Chicago, Cook County, Illinois, United States |
| County formed | Cook County formed 1831 from unorganized territory |
| City incorporated | Chicago incorporated as a city 1837 |
| Fire date | October 8–10, 1871 |
| Statewide vital registration | Illinois did not require statewide birth/death registration until 1916 (county-level Cook County registration began 1871) |

---

## Record Types, Availability, and Access

### 1. Vital Records — Birth, Marriage, Death

**The fire destroyed all pre-1871 locally held vital registers.** Cook County began re-registering vital events immediately after the fire. FamilySearch holds three large indexed collections starting from that watershed:

| Collection | Records | Date Range | FamilySearch ID |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cook County Birth Certificates | 1,450,000 | 1871–1940 | [2024189](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2024189) |
| Cook County Death Records | 980,000 | 1871–1947 | [1913456](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1913456) |
| Cook County Marriage Records | 620,000 | 1871–1920 | [1756321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1756321) |

- **Access level: Indexed + images** (name-searchable on FamilySearch)
- **Original custodian:** Cook County Clerk's Office, 69 W. Washington St., Chicago — vital records from 1871 onward are also available there directly
- **Pre-1871 vital events:** Use church records (see below) as the primary substitute. Illinois statewide registration did not begin until 1916; the FamilySearch Wiki does not state an earlier local-registration date for Cook County beyond what the post-fire series reflects.

---

### 2. Church Records

Church registers are the **most important substitute for pre-1871 vital records** and often the only source for births, marriages, and burials before the courthouse fire. Some parish registers survived the fire; others were re-established from memory or duplicate copies held by denominational headquarters.

| Collection | Records | Date Range | FamilySearch ID |
|---|---|---|---|
| Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records | 285,000 | 1833–1925 | [1803978](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803978) |

- **Access level: Indexed + images** on FamilySearch
- **Catholic parishes:** The **Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives and Records Center** holds surviving Catholic parish registers. Many early Chicago parishes served specific immigrant communities (Irish, German, Polish, Bohemian). Contact: [www.archchicago.org/archives](https://www.archchicago.org/archives)
- **Other denominations:** Check the Chicago History Museum's manuscript collections and the Newberry Library for surviving Methodist, Presbyterian, Lutheran, and other registers
- **Key tip:** If a specific parish register is not on FamilySearch, contact the individual parish — some kept duplicate registers off-site that survived the fire

Source: [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)

---

### 3. Federal Census Records (Critically Important)

The federal census records are among the **most valuable sources for fire-era families** precisely because the originals were held in Washington, D.C. — not Chicago — and thus **survived the fire entirely.**

| Census Year | Notes |
|---|---|
| **1870** | Taken in the months *before* the fire — the single best snapshot of pre-fire Chicago households. Shows names, ages, birthplaces, occupations, real and personal property values. Originals in Washington survived. |
| **1880** | Full post-fire enumeration; shows how families reconstituted after displacement |
| 1850, 1860 | Pre-fire Chicago; originals in Washington, survived |
| 1890 | Substantially destroyed by a separate 1921 Washington fire — a coverage gap |

- **Mortality Schedules (1850–1885):** Record individuals who died in the year preceding each census. The **1880 mortality schedule** covers deaths 1879–1880 and can document fire-related deaths that occurred in the months after the disaster as well as the normal death pattern.
- **Access:** Ancestry.com ([ancestry.com/search/collections/census/](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)) and FamilySearch both hold the federal census; the 1870 census for Chicago is a priority search.

---

### 4. Land and Property Records

Pre-fire deeds were destroyed in the courthouse. Two strategies apply:

**A. Burnt Record Act Re-recordings (post-1872)**
FamilySearch has digitized two relevant volumes:

| Volume | DGS # | Images | Indexed | Searchable | Date Range | Record Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-fire reconstructed copies | 009982110 | 38 | **0%** | No | 1865–1871 | Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed) |
| Post-fire re-recordings | 009982111 | 112 | **41%** | No | 1871–1880 | Post-fire Property Re-recordings |

- Volume 009982110: **Browse-only** — must be viewed image by image with no name search
- Volume 009982111: **Partially indexed** (41%) — search by name for indexed portion; browse remaining images for the rest
- **Total digitized volumes returned by FamilySearch: 2** (this is the complete set for this query window)
- Original re-recorded deeds are also held at the **Cook County Recorder of Deeds**, 118 N. Clark St., Chicago

**B. Chicago Title and Trust Company Records**
Insurance and title records became a critical substitute for destroyed deeds. The **Chicago Title and Trust Company collection** is held at the **Chicago History Museum** and documents pre-fire property ownership. This is a unique resource not available on FamilySearch.
- Chicago History Museum: 1601 N. Clark St., Chicago | [chicagohistory.org](https://www.chicagohistory.org)

**C. Federal Land Patents (BLM General Land Office)**
Original federal patents for land in Illinois are held at the Bureau of Land Management's GLO Records site ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) — created in Washington and not affected by the fire.

Source: [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)

---

### 5. City Directories

City directories are a **premier fire-era substitute** and one of the most underused sources for Chicago research. They document residents by name, occupation, and address — sometimes year by year — allowing you to track a family before, during, and after the fire.

- **Newberry Library** holds Chicago city directories from the **1840s onward** — the longest-running continuous series for the city
- Consecutive directories (e.g., 1870 vs. 1872) reveal who disappeared from a neighborhood, who relocated, and where they re-established themselves after the disaster
- **Newberry Library:** 60 W. Walton St., Chicago | [newberry.org](https://www.newberry.org) — free public access to genealogical collections
- Some directories have been digitized and are searchable on Ancestry.com and the HathiTrust Digital Library

Source: [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)

---

### 6. Court and Probate Records

Pre-fire probate files and court records were largely destroyed in the courthouse. Post-1871 records are substantially intact.

- **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University** holds Cook County records post-1871, including circuit court files, probate records, guardianships, and name changes
  - IRAD Chicago: [library.neiu.edu/irad](https://library.neiu.edu/irad)
- **Naturalization records (pre-1906):** Could be filed in any court of record — federal, state, or local. Chicago naturalizations are at **NARA's Great Lakes Region** (Chicago) facility and at IRAD
- **NARA Great Lakes Region:** 7358 S. Pulaski Rd., Chicago (holds federal court records and many regional naturalization petitions)

---

### 7. Military Records

Military service records, pension files, and draft registrations were held in Washington, D.C. — **not destroyed by the Chicago fire.** This makes them especially valuable for fire-era research.

- **Civil War service records and pension files:** NARA, Washington, D.C.; searchable on [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com) and Ancestry.com
- Many Chicago men served in the Civil War (1861–1865); pension files often include family information, affidavits, and widow's pension records naming children and spouses
- **Draft registrations:** Civil War draft records for Illinois men are at NARA and on Fold3

---

### 8. Newspapers

Chicago newspapers published **extensive coverage of the fire**, including lists of victims, survivors, property losses, and displaced families. Fire-era issues are a unique genealogical source unavailable anywhere else.

- **Chicago Tribune** (1847–present) and **Chicago Inter-Ocean** published fire survivor and victim lists in October–November 1871
- [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) and the **Newberry Library** hold historical Chicago newspaper collections
- The **Chicago History Museum** holds fire-related photographic collections and personal papers documenting individual families' experiences

---

### 9. Cemetery Records

Cemetery record-keeping was independent of the courthouse and largely survived the fire.

- [FindAGrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com) covers major Chicago-area cemeteries (Graceland, Rosehill, Calvary, St. Boniface, and others)
- Many cemeteries have their own records offices — contact them directly for pre-digital burial registers
- Several cemeteries in Chicago predate 1871 and have unbroken records

---

### 10. Immigration and Naturalization

Chicago in 1871 was a heavily immigrant city (German, Irish, Scandinavian, Bohemian communities in particular). Immigration records are held in Washington and thus were not affected by the fire.

- **Passenger arrival lists:** NARA; searchable on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch
- **Naturalization records:** NARA Great Lakes (Chicago), IRAD, and FamilySearch (for microfilmed records)
- **For ethnic-community research:** Denominational archives (e.g., the Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod archives, the Polish Roman Catholic Union archives) often hold parallel registers

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Strongest Holdings for This Period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Cook County vital records (1871+), church records, census, property re-recordings | Free online |
| **Newberry Library** | City directories (1840s+), maps, newspapers, manuscripts | Free in-person |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title & Trust insurance records, photographs, personal papers | In-person; some online |
| **IRAD / Northeastern Illinois Univ.** | Cook County court & probate records post-1871 | In-person |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago Archives** | Catholic parish registers (some pre-fire) | By appointment |
| **NARA Great Lakes Region** | Federal court records, naturalizations, Civil War pension files | In-person / online (Fold3, Ancestry) |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 onward | In-person or mail request |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census, passenger lists, military records | Subscription |

---

## Substitute-Source Strategy (Pre-1871 Gap)

Because the courthouse fire destroyed most official records before October 1871, work the following in priority order for any pre-fire question:

1. **1870 federal census** — taken months before the fire; best pre-fire household snapshot
2. **Church registers** — baptism, marriage, and burial records for the relevant parish
3. **City directories (Newberry Library)** — annual residence and occupation data
4. **Chicago Title and Trust insurance records (Chicago History Museum)** — property ownership
5. **Reconstructed deed volumes on FamilySearch** (DGS 009982110 — browse-only)
6. **1860 and 1850 federal censuses** — earlier household data
7. **Newspapers** — fire coverage, victim/survivor lists, obituaries

---

## Research Quirks and Gotchas

- **Birth/marriage/death collections on FamilySearch all begin in 1871** — this is not an artifact of indexing; pre-fire registers were physically destroyed. Do not expect to find a FamilySearch vital record for a Cook County event before October 1871.
- **The 1870 census for Chicago survived** because the originals were in Washington, D.C. — it is the indispensable pre-fire household document.
- **The 1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed** (by a separate 1921 Washington fire) — use city directories, state censuses, and church records to bridge 1880–1900.
- **Illinois did not require statewide vital registration until 1916.** For 1871–1916, Cook County's own registration (held by the Cook County Clerk) is the civil-registration source; there is no parallel state-level series for this window.
- **Immigrant-community parish registers** often survived separately from official records — always identify the ethnic/religious community and search the relevant denominational archive.
- **The Burnt Record Act re-recordings (DGS 009982111) are only 41% name-indexed** on FamilySearch — if a name search fails, browse the remaining images.
- **FamilySearch wiki_place_page** for Illinois returned only a generic guide for all four sections; the richer Illinois- and Cook County-specific guidance comes from the [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy) page on the FamilySearch Wiki, which you should consult directly.

---

# 🗺️ Locality Research Guide: French Colonial Louisiana (1700s)

**Place:** Louisiana, United States (La Louisiane, French colonial territory)
**Period covered:** ~1699–1769 (French administrative control; Spain begins effective rule c. 1769)
**Produced:** 2026-09-23

---

## Jurisdictional Context

This period spans the entire French colonial era of Louisiana. Key dates that directly affect which records exist and where they are held:

| Date | Event | Research Impact |
|------|-------|----------------|
| 1699 | France establishes permanent settlements (Biloxi, then Mobile) | First colonial records begin |
| 1718 | New Orleans founded by Bienville | St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers begin |
| 1762 | Treaty of Fontainebleau: France secretly cedes Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain; east bank to Britain | Records split by river after this date |
| 1769 | Spain asserts actual administrative control (Governor O'Reilly arrives) | Records begin transitioning to Spanish |

> **Important split:** After 1762, families near the Mississippi River may have generated records on both sides — the west bank under Spain, the east bank (British West Florida/later U.S.) under a different jurisdiction entirely. If your ancestor lived near the river, search both sides. The two-year gap between cession (1762) and Spanish administrative takeover (1769) means some records in this window remain French in form even though technically Spanish territory.

---

## 1. Catholic Parish Registers — **PRIMARY SOURCE for vital events**

**What they contain:** Baptisms (births), marriages, and burial entries. Because the Catholic Church was the *only* legally recognized religion in French Louisiana, parish registers are the sole equivalent of birth, marriage, and death certificates for this period. No civil registration existed.

**The Code Noir:** France's Code Noir required the baptism of all enslaved persons — parish registers therefore document enslaved Africans and their given names, and sometimes name enslavers. This makes registers an essential source for African-descended Louisiana families as well.

**Earliest records:** St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans — sacramental registers survive from **1718**.

**FamilySearch holdings:**
- **Collection: "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** (ID [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)) — This indexed collection covers the colonial period from its beginning in 1718 and is searchable by name. Start here.
- **Digitized volume 004330991** — Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, covering **1720–1803**, 264 images. ⚠️ **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be read image by image. Languages: **French and Spanish.** This complements the indexed collection above and may include images not yet indexed.

**Language warning:** All French colonial registers are in **18th-century French** (with some Latin in formulaic sections). Researchers must be able to read French manuscript hand.

**Physical access:** Original registers are held at the **Louisiana Historical Center** (located in the Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans, LA) and at **St. Louis Cathedral** (New Orleans).

---

## 2. Superior Council Records (Notarial / Court / Estate Records)

The **Conseil Supérieur** (Superior Council) was the principal governing and judicial body of French Louisiana. Its records are among the richest genealogical sources for the colonial period.

**What they contain:**
- Land concessions (grants) to settlers
- Court proceedings and civil suits
- Contracts between colonists
- Estate inventories and succession records (pre-probate court system)
- Marriage contracts

**FamilySearch digitized volume:**
- **Volume 004330992** — "French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records)," covering **1699–1769**, 149 images. ⚠️ **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Languages: **French and Spanish.** Must be browsed image by image.

**FamilySearch indexed collection (partial overlap):**
- **"Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984"** (ID [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)) — begins 1756, so the last ~13 years of the French colonial period are covered with name-indexed records.

**Physical access:** The bulk of these records are held at the **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) and have been **partially** digitized. Contact the Center directly for access to undigitized material.

---

## 3. Notarial Records

New Orleans is home to the **oldest continuous notarial office in North America.** Notarial acts from the **1730s onward** document:
- Property sales and transfers
- Marriage settlements (contrats de mariage)
- Wills and testaments
- Business contracts

**Access:** The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** is open to the public. Many pre–Civil War notarial records have been microfilmed. Note that the Superior Council records (above) overlap in function with notarial acts for the early colonial period, before a separate notarial system was fully established.

Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)), these records are available at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center.

---

## 4. Land Records

**French concessions** (land grants) in colonial Louisiana followed French legal tradition — not English common law. These are documented in:
- **American State Papers: Public Lands** series (available digitally via various repositories including HathiTrust and Congress.gov) — records claims and confirmations after the U.S. acquired Louisiana in 1803, but references original French grants
- **Louisiana State Land Office** — holds original survey and grant records

Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)), the French concession system is documented in both these series and the Superior Council records listed above.

⚠️ **No FamilySearch volume_search results** specifically for land/property records of the 1700–1769 window came back beyond the Superior Council volume above. Physical repositories are likely the primary access point.

---

## 5. Colonial Census Rolls (Recensements)

The French colonial administration periodically counted settlements. These rolls can document household members, including servants and enslaved persons.

**Where held:** The **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)** in Aix-en-Provence, France is the primary repository for colonial administrative records including census rolls. ANOM also holds administrative correspondence naming settlers, officials, soldiers, and colonists.

**Access:** ANOM provides online catalog access at [anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr). Some materials can be ordered as digital scans. Records are in **French.** No FamilySearch digitization of ANOM materials appeared in tool results — this is a significant gap for online access.

---

## 6. Military Records

French colonial Louisiana had a garrison of soldiers and a local militia. Colonial military muster rolls and officer lists survive in the ANOM (Aix-en-Provence). If your ancestor was a soldier or officer, ANOM is the place to look.

The **National Archives (NARA)** — returned by external link search — holds later U.S. records but does not cover the French colonial period itself.

---

## 7. Vital Records (Civil Registration)

> **There is no civil registration for the French colonial period.** Catholic parish registers (Section 1 above) are the complete substitute. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return Louisiana-specific vital registration start dates in tool results; the Louisiana-specific wiki pages returned generic content rather than Louisiana detail. What is confirmed: statewide civil registration came much later than 1769, and no civil system operated during French rule.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|------------|--------------|--------|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Church Records 1718–1925 (indexed); Probate Records 1756+ (indexed); 2 browse-only volumes (sacramental registers + Superior Council notarial acts) | Free online |
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records; parish register originals; partially digitized | In-person / contact for digital |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | Notarial acts from 1730s onward | Public access, in-person |
| **St. Louis Cathedral**, New Orleans | Original sacramental registers from 1718 | Contact parish |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France | Administrative correspondence; colonial census rolls; military musters | Online catalog; digital scans on request |
| **Louisiana State Land Office** | Land concession records | Contact office |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Later federal records only; not applicable to French colonial period | Online / in-person |

---

## Key Quirks and Gotchas

1. **Language:** All French colonial records are in **18th-century French manuscript**. Some post-1762 records mix in Spanish as administration transitioned. Budget time for transcription or hire a specialist.
2. **No civil registration:** For baptisms, marriages, and burials, Catholic parish registers are the *only* source — treat them as birth/marriage/death certificates.
3. **West/East Mississippi split after 1762:** If your family lived near the Mississippi, search both the Spanish (west bank) and British/American (east bank) sides after 1762. Which successor jurisdiction holds a given record depends on exactly where within the original territory the event occurred; search both rather than assuming one side.
4. **Enslaved persons in parish registers:** The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved people — registers document them, often by given name only, and name the enslaver. This is frequently the *only* contemporary record of enslaved individuals.
5. **French dit names:** Colonial Louisiana families often used *dit* (alias) names — a secondary surname by which a family was also known. Records may index a family under either name. Check both.
6. **Indexed vs. browse-only on FamilySearch:** The "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" collection is name-searchable, but the two digitized volumes (004330991 and 004330992) are 0% indexed and must be browsed image-by-image — a time-intensive process.
7. **ANOM is the essential complement to FamilySearch:** Colonial census rolls and administrative records exist only in France. FamilySearch does not appear to have digitized ANOM holdings for this period based on tool results.
8. **Superior Council records cover 1699–1769 in one FamilySearch volume (004330992)** — this single 149-image browse-only volume may hold the only digitized copy of notarial/court records for the entire French colonial period.

---

## Recommended Starting Sequence

1. **Start with FamilySearch:** Search the indexed **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** (collection 1612905) for your surnames. This is the fastest entry point.
2. **Browse the colonial volumes:** If the indexed search doesn't find your ancestor, browse volumes **004330991** (sacramental registers, 1720–1803) and **004330992** (Superior Council notarial acts, 1699–1769) image by image on FamilySearch.
3. **Search probate records:** If ancestor appears after 1756, check "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341) on FamilySearch.
4. **Contact the Louisiana Historical Center:** For Superior Council records not yet digitized or for fuller access to parish registers.
5. **Visit or contact NARA-ANOM:** For colonial census rolls, administrative correspondence, and military records held in France — essential for a complete picture.
6. **Check the New Orleans Notarial Archives** for contracts, marriage settlements, and wills from the 1730s onward.

---

*Sources: FamilySearch collections_search, volume_search, and wiki_search results; Wikipedia article "French Louisiana"; FamilySearch Wiki pages [Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records) and [Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants). Note: FamilySearch wiki_place_page for Louisiana returned generic content rather than Louisiana-specific pages across all four sections — Louisiana-specific wiki detail was obtained via wiki_search instead.*

The ANOM in France is an irreplaceable complement for census and administrative records that haven't made it online. # 🪨 Locality Research Guide: Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns, Late 1800s (c. 1870–1906)

**Scope:** This guide covers both the **Anthracite Coal Region** of northeastern Pennsylvania (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties) and the **Bituminous Coal Region** of western Pennsylvania (Cambria, Westmoreland, Fayette, Allegheny, and surrounding counties). The target period is roughly 1870–1906 — from the first Mine Inspector reports to the start of statewide vital registration.

---

## Jurisdictional Context

| County | Type | Formed | Region |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Schuylkill** | Anthracite | 1811 | NE PA |
| **Luzerne** | Anthracite | Earlier (parent of Lackawanna) | NE PA |
| **Lackawanna** | Anthracite | **1878**, carved from Luzerne | NE PA |
| **Carbon** | Anthracite | — | NE PA |
| **Cambria** | Bituminous | 1804 | W PA |
| **Westmoreland** | Bituminous | 1773 | W PA |

> ⚠️ **Critical boundary note:** Lackawanna County did not exist until 1878. All records for Scranton and surrounding communities before that date were filed under **Luzerne County**. If your ancestor lived in Lackawanna County territory before 1878, search Luzerne County records first, then Lackawanna from 1878 onward — these form one continuous research trail despite the different county names.

According to Wikipedia, Pennsylvania was the leading coal-producing state throughout the 19th century. Mining communities drew massive immigrant waves: **Irish, Welsh, German, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, and Italian** families all settled the region, each community centered on its own ethnic parishes and fraternal organizations. The Avondale Mine disaster (1869, 110 dead) prompted Pennsylvania's first mine safety legislation; the Molly Maguires (Irish immigrant activists) were active in the 1870s — court records from their trials are a notable genealogical source.

---

## ⚠️ The Single Most Important Fact for This Period

**Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1906.**

*(Source: [Pennsylvania Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))*

This means for the late 1800s target period:
- **No state birth or death certificates exist** for most families
- Births and deaths were recorded, if at all, by **churches** or a handful of individual counties (Philadelphia from 1860, Allegheny County from 1870)
- **Church records are the primary vital record source** for this era

---

## Record Types

### 1. 📜 Vital Records

| Record | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Births / Deaths** | Church records only (no state registration until 1906) | Physical/microfilm; some digitized |
| **County Marriages** | Colonial period onward at county level | FamilySearch collections (see below) |
| **Death Certificates** | 1906 onward only | FamilySearch: [Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317) — starts *after* the target period |

**FamilySearch collections for marriage records (overlapping target period):**
- [Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) — 524,189 records
- [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) — 312,045 records
- [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) — 198,765 records (index only, no images)

**Bottom line:** For births and deaths in the 1870s–1900s, go to church records first. Marriage licenses and bonds are at county courthouses and on FamilySearch.

---

### 2. ⛏️ Mine & Occupational Records — The Records You Won't Find Elsewhere

These are the most distinctive sources for coal mining ancestry and are often overlooked:

**State Mine Inspector Reports (from 1870)**
Published annually by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. They list **fatal mine accidents by name, age, nationality, and cause of death.** This is one of the few official pre-1906 sources that documents deaths of miners by name. Held at the Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg.
*(Source: [Pennsylvania Occupational Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))*

**Company Employment Records (Payrolls, Accident Reports)**
Survive fragmentarily at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** and at **local historical societies** in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties. Coverage is uneven — not all companies' records survived.

**FamilySearch Digitized Volumes (first page of 23 total):**

| Volume | Place | Date Range | Record Type | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [002240015](https://www.familysearch.org/search/image/index?owc=002240015) | Schuylkill County | 1870–1900 | Mine Worker Employment Cards | ✅ **Indexed + full-text searchable** (95% indexed, 410 images) |
| [002240016](https://www.familysearch.org/search/image/index?owc=002240016) | Luzerne County | 1870–1895 | Mine Accident Reports | ⚠️ **Browse-only** (0% indexed, 287 images) |
| [002240017](https://www.familysearch.org/search/image/index?owc=002240017) | Lackawanna County | 1878–1900 | Colliery Payroll Ledgers | ⚠️ **Browse-only** (0% indexed, 199 images) |

> **Note:** The volume search returned 23 total digitized volumes for this region/period. Only the 3 above are from the first page of results. Ask for more if you want the full list.

**Union Records — UMWA**
The United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890) maintained membership rolls and grievance files. These can place an ancestor in a specific colliery at a specific date.
*(Source: [Pennsylvania Occupational Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))*

---

### 3. ✝️ Church Records — Your Primary Vital Source

Because statewide registration did not exist until 1906, **ethnic parish registers are often the only record of births, baptisms, marriages, and burials.** Each immigrant community typically formed its own congregation:

| Ethnic Community | Typical Denomination |
|---|---|
| Irish | Roman Catholic |
| Welsh | Congregational / Presbyterian / Baptist |
| Polish | Roman Catholic (Polish-language parishes) |
| Lithuanian | Roman Catholic (Lithuanian-language parishes) |
| Slovak | Roman Catholic or Lutheran |
| German | Lutheran, Reformed, or Catholic |
| Italian | Roman Catholic |

> ⚠️ **Language warning:** Records from Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, and German parishes may be written in those languages, not English. Plan accordingly.

Church registers are held variously at: the individual parish, diocesan archives, the **Historical Society of Schuylkill County**, the **Lackawanna County Historical Society**, and on FamilySearch microfilm. The FamilySearch wiki_read for the Pennsylvania Church Records page returned generic content and did not provide Pennsylvania-specific digitization details — consult the [Pennsylvania Church Records FamilySearch Wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records) directly for current holdings.

---

### 4. 🧾 Census Records

Federal censuses covering the target period are fully indexed and widely available:

| Year | Notes |
|---|---|
| **1870** | Lists occupation; "miner" identifies coal mining families |
| **1880** | Adds relationship-to-head; identifies specific mine employer in some cases |
| **1890** | *Destroyed by fire* — almost entirely lost |
| **1900** | Adds immigration year and years in the US — critical for immigrant miners |

The 1880 and 1900 **Soundex indexes** help locate immigrant miners with anglicized or variant-spelled names. **Mortality schedules** (1850–1880) record deaths in the year preceding each census and can substitute for missing death certificates.

---

### 5. 🛳️ Immigration & Naturalization

Most coal-region immigrants arrived through **Philadelphia** and **New York** ports. Passenger lists from both ports are indexed on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch for this period.

**Naturalization records** before 1906 were filed in *any court of record* — county courts, federal courts, and state courts all granted citizenship. Search all of them, not just federal courts.

- **Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906):** Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**, Harrisburg.
- For Luzerne/Lackawanna: check county courthouse records and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
*(Source: [Pennsylvania Occupational Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))*

The FamilySearch collections for Pennsylvania include:
- [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) — 893,214 records (also useful for estate files naming heirs)

---

### 6. 🏠 Land & Probate Records

*(Source: [Pennsylvania Land Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))*

Mining families often rented company-owned housing (patch towns), so they may not appear in deed books as landowners. However:
- **The Pennsylvania Land Office** (Harrisburg) holds warrant, survey, and patent records from William Penn's grants onward
- **County deed books** begin at county formation and are held at county courthouses
- **Probate records** (wills, inventories, guardianships) are at the county Register of Wills from the colonial period onward; FamilySearch has indexed these in [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)
- **Tax assessment lists** survive from the 1690s in some Pennsylvania counties and serve as census substitutes

---

### 7. ⚖️ Court Records

Court records are particularly valuable for the coal region because of the concentration of labor unrest:
- **Naturalization petitions** and declarations of intent in county courts
- **Criminal and civil trial records** — including Molly Maguires trials (1870s–1880s) in Carbon and Schuylkill County courts
- Guardianship and estate files naming minor children
- **Mine disaster inquests** (coroner's records) when fatalities occurred

---

### 8. 🪖 Military Records

Veterans of the Civil War (1861–1865) appear in:
- **Service records and pension files** at NARA (Fold3.com has many digitized)
- **Pennsylvania Volunteer rosters** at the Pennsylvania State Archives
- **GAR (Grand Army of the Republic) post records** — many coal towns had GAR posts

Spanish-American War veterans (1898) also appear in federal service records.

---

### 9. 📰 Newspapers & Cemetery Records

- **Historical newspapers** from coal towns (the *Miners' Journal* of Pottsville is particularly notable for Schuylkill County) carried death notices, accident reports, and community news. Available on Newspapers.com and through the Pennsylvania State Library.
- **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) indexes many coal-region cemeteries
- **Cemetery transcriptions** are also held at county historical societies

---

## 🏛️ Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Naturalization records, Mine Inspector reports, state-level records |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) | Local mining records, church transcriptions, newspapers |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum** (Scranton / Lackawanna) | Mining community collections, ethnic community records |
| **Lackawanna County Historical Society** | County-level records, local collections |
| **County Courthouses** | Deeds, marriages, probate, naturalization petitions |
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Census, marriage, probate collections; 23+ digitized mining volumes |
| **NARA** (Philadelphia regional; also online) | Passenger lists, naturalization, military pension files |
| **Ancestry.com** | Census, passenger lists, military records |
| **Fold3.com** | Civil War service records and pensions |
| **Newspapers.com** | *Miners' Journal* and other regional papers |
| **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records |

---

## 🔑 Research Quirks & Watchouts

1. **No state birth/death certificates before 1906.** Church records are the substitute — identify the ethnic parish your ancestor likely attended before searching.
2. **Lackawanna County didn't exist before 1878.** Search Luzerne County records for Scranton-area events before that year.
3. **Ethnic parish records may be in a foreign language.** Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, and German registers are common; be prepared to read or translate them.
4. **Mine Inspector reports (from 1870) name accident victims.** These are often the only official record of a miner's death before 1906 — essential for fatal mining accidents.
5. **Miners often lived in company-owned "patch towns."** They may not appear in property records as landowners; look for them in census, church, and company employment records instead.
6. **Pre-1906 naturalization records are scattered across any court of record** — not just federal courts. Search county, state, and federal courts.
7. **The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed.** Use 1880 and 1900 to bridge the gap; check city directories, tax lists, and church records for the decade.
8. **Union records (UMWA, founded 1890) can place ancestors at a specific colliery.** Check the UMWA archives alongside company records.
9. **Adjacent county research is essential.** Families frequently crossed county lines; Carbon and Northumberland counties adjoin the main anthracite region. For the bituminous region, Fayette, Washington, and Indiana counties neighbor Cambria and Westmoreland. Search neighboring counties for the same individuals.

---

## Locality Research Guide: Massachusetts — Early Puritan Settlements (c. 1620–1700)

### Jurisdictional Context

Two **separate colonial jurisdictions** governed what is now Massachusetts during this period. You must search both:

| Jurisdiction | Active | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Plymouth Colony** | 1620–1691 | Founded by the Pilgrim Separatists; merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691 |
| **Massachusetts Bay Colony** | 1628–1691 | Founded by Puritan reformers; dominant jurisdiction for the Great Migration (c. 1630–1643) |
| **Province of Massachusetts Bay** | 1691–1776 | Royal charter uniting Plymouth, Massachusetts Bay, and Maine |

Plymouth Colony records are **published and indexed separately** from Massachusetts Bay Colony records — searching only one will miss a substantial portion of colonial families. *(FamilySearch Wiki: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))*

Massachusetts Bay Colony created four counties in **1643** (Suffolk, Middlesex, Essex, Norfolk). Before 1643, records were filed at the colony level, not the county level. Plymouth Colony had its own county structure (Plymouth, Barnstable, Bristol).

---

### Record Types, Availability, and Access

#### 1. 🏛 Town Vital Records — **Indexed + Images** ★★★
**FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) (Collection ID 2061550) — name-indexed with images.

Massachusetts Bay Colony required towns to record births, marriages, and deaths beginning in **1639** (town level). This is one of the earliest mandatory civil registration systems in North America. *(Wikipedia: [Massachusetts Bay Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony))*

A critical published finding aid is the **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series** (Tanner–Corbin series), which abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns. This should be your first stop for any pre-1850 Massachusetts ancestor. *(FamilySearch Wiki: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))*

> ⚠️ **Gap before 1639:** For events before the 1639 mandate, town records may not exist. Church records (see below) are often the only surviving source for births/baptisms, marriages, and burials in the earliest years.

---

#### 2. ⛪ Church Records — **Indexed + Images; also Browse-Only volume**
**FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) (Collection ID 1921657) — name-indexed with images, starts 1630.

**FamilySearch digitized volume (browse/full-text):**
- Image Group **007612045** — 121 images covering **Suffolk County, Massachusetts, 1630–1700**, record type: *Congregational church admissions and baptisms*
  - 🔍 **Full-text searchable, NOT name-indexed** — reachable via full-text search but not by name search. No ability to browse by surname.

Congregational churches were the **established church** of the Puritan colony. Their registers are central to early Massachusetts genealogy and include:
- Baptisms and membership admissions
- Marriages
- Burials
- Disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments)

Many early church records have been published in the **Colonial Society of Massachusetts** series and in local historical society volumes. *(FamilySearch Wiki: [Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))*

---

#### 3. 📜 Probate Records — **Indexed + Images** ★★★
**FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) (Collection ID 1678901) — name-indexed with images, starts 1635.

Probate records began at the county level from the **1630s**. *(FamilySearch Wiki: [Massachusetts Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))* They include wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, and letters of administration — extremely valuable for identifying heirs, family relationships, and property in this period.

---

#### 4. 🌾 Land Records — **Browse-Only Images** (FamilySearch); Physical at County Registries
**FamilySearch digitized volume (browse-only):**
- Image Group **007612044** — 188 images covering **Massachusetts, 1620–1698**, record type: *Town meeting and proprietors' records*
  - ⚠️ **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, NOT full-text searchable. Must be browsed image-by-image.

Land deeds were recorded at the **county registries of deeds from the 1630s**, in remarkably complete runs. *(FamilySearch Wiki: [Massachusetts Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))*  Proprietors' records (town land grants) are especially important for the earliest settlers.

Physical originals are held at **county registries of deeds** (one per county). The Massachusetts Archives also holds colony-era land grants.

---

#### 5. 🏛 Court & Colony Records — **Physical; partial digitization**
The **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) holds the original Massachusetts Bay Colony records from the 1620s onward, including:
- Governor's correspondence
- General Court (legislature) records
- Colony-level court records

These are partially available on microfilm through FamilySearch but the FamilySearch volume search returned only 2 volumes specifically covering 1620–1700, so physical or microfilm access remains essential for deep colonial research.

---

#### 6. 🧭 The Great Migration Study — **Published Reference** ★★★
The **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** in Boston (nehgs.org) holds the most comprehensive genealogical library in New England for this period, including:
- Manuscript collections
- Published genealogies
- The **Great Migration** study series — documenting every known settler who arrived in Massachusetts 1620–1643, with sources and citations

*(FamilySearch Wiki: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))*

This is an essential secondary source for anyone with Puritan immigrant ancestors.

---

#### 7. 📋 Census Records — **NOT available for this period**
Federal census records begin in **1790** — nearly 90 years after this period ends. No colonial census enumeration exists for early Massachusetts. Do not expect census records as a source here.

---

#### 8. 🪖 Military Records
**Fold3** (fold3.com) holds colonial militia and military records. For the early Puritan period, relevant records include King Philip's War (1675–1676) muster rolls and colonial militia lists, which can document male heads of household.

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives, Boston** | Colony court, governor, and land records from 1620s | In person; partial microfilm via FamilySearch |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** | Manuscript collections, Great Migration series, published genealogies | In person (Boston); online via americanancestors.org |
| **County Registries of Deeds** | Deed books from 1630s | In person at each county courthouse |
| **County Probate Courts** | Probate files from 1630s | In person; partially digitized on FamilySearch |
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Town Vital Records (indexed), Church Records (indexed), Probate Records (indexed), plus browse-only volumes | Free online |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Federal records (mostly post-period); colonial militia via state adjutant general | archives.gov |
| **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records and transcriptions | Free online |

---

### ⚠️ Researcher Quirks & Gotchas

1. **Two colonies, two record systems.** Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628–1691) were entirely separate governments. A family in Plymouth had records kept under Plymouth Colony jurisdiction; search both independently. Plymouth Colony records are published and indexed separately.

2. **Town vital recording began 1639 at the town level.** Events before 1639 typically appear only in Congregational church registers, not town books.

3. **Counties were created in 1643.** Before 1643, Massachusetts Bay Colony records were kept at the colony level, not the county level. Search the colony/state level, not a specific county, for pre-1643 events.

4. **The Tanner–Corbin "Vital Records to 1850" series is your roadmap.** This multi-volume published series covers 200+ towns and is where most researchers start. Check NEHGS and your state library system.

5. **Congregational church records are the established-church record.** For Puritan-era families, this is the functional equivalent of a parish register elsewhere. Membership in a congregation was a civic requirement.

6. **The FamilySearch volume search returned only 2 digitized volumes for 1620–1700.** Both are browse-only or full-text only (not name-indexed). The indexed collections (Town Vital Records, Church Records, Probate) are the primary online search entry points for this period.

7. **No Wikipedia or FamilySearch Wiki pages were returned with Massachusetts-specific content** from the place-page tool in this session (all returned a generic fallback guide). For current FamilySearch Wiki guidance, visit [Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy) and [Massachusetts Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records) directly.

---

### Recommended Research Sequence

1. **Start with the Great Migration study** (NEHGS) to confirm your ancestor's arrival date and first colony.
2. **Search town vital records** on FamilySearch (Collection 2061550) for 1639 and later.
3. **Search church records** (Collection 1921657) — especially for events before 1639 or for families documented only in congregational registers.
4. **Check probate records** (Collection 1678901) — estate files often name spouse, children, and neighbors.
5. **Browse proprietors' and town meeting records** (Image Group 007612044, browse-only, 188 images, 1620–1698) for land grants to first-generation settlers.
6. **Visit Massachusetts Archives and NEHGS in person** for colony court records, manuscript collections, and unpublished materials not yet digitized.
7. **If your family was in Plymouth Colony**, treat it as a separate jurisdiction and consult the published Plymouth Colony Records series.

Now I have the standardPlace. Let me run the full parallel survey batch:

Here is your locality research guide for tracing families in Oklahoma during the Land Run era.

---

# 🏃 Oklahoma Locality Research Guide: Land Run Era (c. 1880–1910)

## Jurisdictional Context

Oklahoma passed through three distinct legal jurisdictions during this period, and each generated its own record series. This is the most important structural fact for your research:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Implication for Records |
|---|---|---|
| Before May 2, 1890 | Indian Territory / Federal (Unassigned Lands) | No county structure; records are federal or tribal |
| May 2, 1890 – Nov. 16, 1907 | **Oklahoma Territory** | County structure established; territorial courts, marriages, tax rolls begin |
| Nov. 16, 1907 onward | **State of Oklahoma** | Statewide vital registration begins (1908) |

The Land Run of April 22, 1889 opened ~2 million acres of Unassigned Lands; an estimated 50,000 settlers participated. Homestead claims were administered by the federal General Land Office through two land offices: **Guthrie** and **Kingfisher**. Oklahoma Territory was formally organized by the Organic Act on May 2, 1890, with Guthrie as capital. Oklahoma and Indian Territory merged into the state on November 16, 1907.

---

## ⭐ Record Type 1: Federal Homestead / Land Records — Your Anchor Source

Every legitimate Land Run claimant filed a homestead application. These files typically contain:
- The original application (settler's name, age, prior state of residence)
- Affidavits from **two witnesses** (often neighbors or relatives — cross-reference for social networks)
- Proof of five years' residence and improvement
- The final land patent
- **Rejected and contested applications also survive** and often contain richer family detail, including "Sooner" accusation hearings with witness testimony

**Where to find them:**

- **FamilySearch** — "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (collection ID 1541872): 234,567 records, 117,283 images — **indexed + images**, free at familysearch.org
- **FamilySearch digitized volume** (image group 005221388): 402 images of land-entry case files and homestead final proofs, 1889–1907 — **74% name-indexed**, not full-text searchable
- **BLM General Land Office Records** — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — free searchable database of federal land patents and survey plats for Oklahoma
- **National Archives, Washington D.C.** — Record Group 49 (General Land Office): original case files; order through [archives.gov](https://archives.gov)

---

## Record Type 2: Indian / Tribal Records and Dawes Commission Rolls

Essential for any family with Native American ancestry, or who lived in eastern Oklahoma (Indian Territory), home to the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole). The Dawes Commission (1893–1907) was required to enroll tribal citizens for land allotment; enrollment was mandatory for citizenship claims and allotments.

- **FamilySearch** — "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection ID 1987432): 567,890 records, 283,945 images — **indexed + images**, free
- **FamilySearch digitized volume** (image group 005221389): 176 images of Dawes Commission enrollment jackets, 1898–1910 — **⚠️ 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image.** Jackets contain name, age, family relationships, and freedmen (formerly enslaved tribal members)
- **National Archives at Fort Worth** — Dawes Commission records, Bureau of Indian Affairs records, Indian school records for Five Civilized Tribes
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — extensive Indian Territory and tribal records holdings

---

## Record Type 3: Census Records

| Census | Notes | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **1880 Federal** | Most Land Run settlers were living elsewhere 9 years before the run — this is your primary tool for finding the family *before* Oklahoma | FamilySearch (free), Ancestry, MyHeritage |
| **1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census** ⭐ | Rare survival: most 1890 federal census records burned in 1921, but Oklahoma Territory had a **special territorial enumeration** that survives. Documents early Land Run settlers by name | Oklahoma Historical Society, Guthrie |
| **1900 Federal** | ⚠️ **Critical split**: Oklahoma Territory (west) and Indian Territory (east) were enumerated as **two separate entities**. A family in eastern Oklahoma appears under "Indian Territory," not "Oklahoma Territory." Search both | FamilySearch (free), Ancestry, MyHeritage |
| **1910 Federal** | Post-statehood; Oklahoma is a single state | FamilySearch (free), Ancestry, MyHeritage |

---

## Record Type 4: Marriage Records

- **FamilySearch** — "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" (collection ID 2134789): 456,789 records, 913,578 persons, 228,394 images — **indexed + images**, free
- Begins 1890, when county governments were first organized under Oklahoma Territory
- Marriages before 1890 in the Unassigned Lands: look to church records or departure-state records

---

## Record Type 5: Vital Records (Births & Deaths)

⚠️ **Gap warning:** Oklahoma's statewide vital registration did not begin until **1908** (the year after statehood). Before 1908, look for births and deaths in:
- Church registers (see below)
- Newspaper birth announcements and obituaries
- Tombstone inscriptions (FindAGrave — [findagrave.com](https://findagrave.com))
- Family Bible records
- County coroner records (spotty)

---

## Record Type 6: Church Records

- **FamilySearch** — "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (collection ID 1654321): 123,456 records, 61,728 images — **indexed + images**, free. Pre-1889 records are primarily mission records serving Native communities
- Church records begin **sporadically in 1889** as denominations established congregations in new Land Run towns — Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian denominations were among the first in Guthrie and Oklahoma City
- **Denominational archives** — Contact national denomination archives (United Methodist Archives, American Baptist Historical Society, etc.) for early congregation records not yet microfilmed
- Church records *before 1889* for families in Indian Territory are found under Five Civilized Tribes mission records in the pre-1890 range

---

## Record Type 7: Territorial Court Records

Territorial district court records (Oklahoma Territory, 1890–1907) contain civil and criminal cases, **probate records** (wills, estate inventories, guardianships), and **naturalization records**. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record.

- **National Archives at Fort Worth** — primary repository for federal territorial court records
- **Oklahoma State Archives** (Oklahoma City) — state and territorial records, county-level court records on microfilm

---

## Record Type 8: Tax Records

County personal property and real estate tax rolls from the 1890s forward can fill the gap between the 1889 Land Run and the 1900 census, confirming a family's year-by-year presence on their claim.

- **County courthouses** and **Oklahoma State Archives**

---

## Record Type 9: Military Records

Many Land Run settlers were Civil War veterans. **Pension files** at NARA often include detailed family histories, marriage documentation, and widow's pension applications with children's names and ages. Search departure-state service records first.

- **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://fold3.com), subscription) — digitized military records, pension files, service records
- **NARA** ([archives.gov](https://archives.gov)) — original pension files; order online

---

## Record Type 10: Newspapers

Oklahoma Territory towns had newspapers almost from the first day of the Land Run (Guthrie had papers by late April 1889). Early papers published arrival lists, homestead claim notices, legal notices, and personal items.

- **Newspapers.com** (subscription) — full-text searchable historical Oklahoma newspapers
- **Chronicling America** ([chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov)) — free; includes early Oklahoma Territory papers from the Library of Congress
- **Oklahoma Digital Newspaper Program** (Oklahoma Historical Society) — free online access to many territorial-era papers

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives at Fort Worth** | Federal territorial court records (1890–1907), Dawes/BIA records | In-person or NARA online ordering |
| **National Archives, Washington D.C.** | GLO homestead case files (RG 49), military pensions | In-person or online ordering |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** (OKC) | 1890 territorial census, newspapers, territorial records | On-site; some digitized at OklahomaHistory.org |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** (OKC) | State/territorial government records, county records on microfilm | On-site; some online |
| **BLM GLO Records** | Federal land patents | Free: glorecords.blm.gov |
| **FamilySearch** | 4 indexed collections; 2 digitized volumes (see table below) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census, additional records | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military records | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery records | Free |

---

## FamilySearch Collections at a Glance

| Collection | ID | Date Range | Records | Digitization Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records | 1541872 | 1834–1907 | 234,567 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls | 1987432 | 1851–1959 | 567,890 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Oklahoma, County Marriages | 2134789 | 1890–1995 | 456,789 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records | 1654321 | 1820–1965 | 123,456 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Homestead final proofs (vol. 005221388) | — | 1889–1907 | 402 images | ✅ 74% indexed + images |
| Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (vol. 005221389) | — | 1898–1910 | 176 images | ⚠️ **Browse-only (0% indexed)** |

---

## ⚠️ Critical Research Quirks

1. **"Oklahoma" didn't legally exist before May 2, 1890.** Records before that date are under "Indian Territory" or direct federal jurisdiction. Searching "Oklahoma" in databases before 1890 will miss records indexed under those earlier jurisdictions.

2. **Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory remained separate through 1907.** Eastern Oklahoma records generated 1890–1907 are under "Indian Territory," not "Oklahoma Territory." The 1900 census reflects this split sharply.

3. **Always trace the family backward before searching Oklahoma.** Land Run settlers arrived from somewhere. The **1880 federal census** — nine years before the run — is your primary tool for finding the family of origin. The most common origin states were Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and Arkansas. Search departure-state vital, land, and church records first, then follow them into Oklahoma.

4. **Witness affidavits in homestead proofs name neighbors** — often relatives or people who traveled together. Cross-reference the homestead filings on neighboring quarter-sections to reconstruct a migration network.

5. **Rejected and contested applications survive** at NARA alongside approved claims and may contain richer detail, including full testimonies naming family members and co-migrants.
